item.title: Congressional Black Caucus plays hardball with Jeffries-skeptic DSA Democrats
item.description:
Some members of the Congressional Black Caucus want a condition for incoming Democrats seeking to join their ranks: You have to support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker.

Why it matters: Things could get dicey fast, as several Black Democrats who are all but guaranteed to be elected in November have declined to commit to voting for Jeffries.

  • But Darializa Avila Chevalier wants in: The Afro-Latino nominee in New York's 13th District told Semafor she will seek to join both the CBC and the Hispanic Caucus if elected.
  • Pennsylvania state Rep. Chris Rabb, the nominee for a Philadelphia-based House seat, told Axios he is "definitely planning to join" the CBC.
  • "I absolutely plan on joining the Black Caucus," said Melat Kiros of Colorado — another Black Democrat running in a safely blue district.

All three DSA-aligned candidates have declined to commit to voting for Jeffries as speaker.

  • Kiros previously told Axios she "will not vote for any Democrat for a leadership position if they take corporate PAC money," which would apply to Jeffries.

What we're hearing: Several members of the Black Caucus, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer frank remarks about likely incoming colleagues, said criticism of Democratic leadership could be an issue.

  • One senior CBC member, when asked if Avila Chevalier would be allowed to join, told Axios: "Not if she doesn't support Hakeem along with other issues."
  • Asked if that would apply to all incoming members, the lawmaker replied, "Yes."
  • Avila Chevalier "absolutely will not be welcomed if she doesn't support Hakeem," said a second CBC member. "Under no circumstances would anyone be welcomed with a warm embrace if they are going to undermine the brotha! Just no path."

Between the lines: Loyalty to Democratic leadership isn't a formal criterion for CBC membership, a source familiar with the matter told Axios, but it may be a de facto one.

  • "Support for Hakeem is not a written rule, at least not yet," the source said, but "it would be a challenge to accept someone in the CBC who doesn't support him for speaker."
  • The source added: "The CBC has far-left people, Squad members, DSA members. ... But they are committed to Black people and the Black agenda. Hakeem Jeffries as speaker of the House is about progress for Black people and the Black agenda."
  • "You can't come to the CBC and blow up the point of the CBC. It does not make sense."

Yes, but: The second House Democrat who spoke on the condition of anonymity stressed that while these members may not be welcomed with open arms, it doesn't mean they will be turned away entirely.

  • "We have had Republicans," the lawmaker noted. The CBC allowed former GOP Rep. Mia Love to join, though it has denied other Republicans.
  • The group has also rebuffed some Democrats, including Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.), the Afro-Latino chair of the Hispanic Caucus, whom Avila Chevalier unseated in June.

A Democratic leadership source strongly pushed back against the notion that any incoming Black Democrats would be denied entry to the CBC based on their vote for speaker.

  • "I don't believe the CBC decides its membership based on one's pledge to support leadership," the source said, adding that Avila Chevalier "will get the same review process as everyone else."
  • "I don't think it's a thing at the end of the day," the source said.

The bottom line: "As with every new Congress, matters related to membership for the 120th Congress will be addressed following the 2026 election cycle through the Congressional Black Caucus's established processes," a CBC spokesperson told Axios.

  • "Right now, our focus is on voting rights while remaining committed to advancing policies that expand opportunity, protect fundamental rights, and improve the lives of the communities we serve."

item.title: Max Miller doubles down on staying in Ohio House race
item.description:
Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) said Tuesday that he won't drop his reelection bid despite facing allegations of domestic abuse and violence from his ex-wife and two other women.

Why it matters: Miller has until Wednesday to withdraw from the race, and President Trump has expressed concern that the embattled congressman could put a reliably Republican seat at risk in the midterms.

What they're saying: When asked about his plans on Tuesday by CNN's Jake Tapper, Miller said he wouldn't withdraw, and pointed to Trump as a reason why.

  • "In 2016, when President Donald J. Trump faced the most extreme allegations in the world that hit him day after day after day, and people in the media, very much like yourself and others, said that he would have no shot at winning, that he should not be the president of the United States. But guess what? He stayed in, and he was resilient."
  • "And what the American people can see, is ....somebody is fighting, who is resilient, and that is a quality that the American people cherish," Miller said.

The intrigue: Miller acknowledged that Trump called him Monday and asked if Miller could still win this November.

  • "He said, 'I don't know if you're going to be able to pull this one out.'" Miller said. "I reminded him of the same resilience that he had when people told him that he was going to struggle in 2016, and he became the 45th president of the United States."
  • "I have the utmost confidence that my constituents back home know me. This race is a home race. This isn't about what the national media thinks."

Zoom out: Miller also said "more than 50% of the people within this country who are divorced."

  • Roughly one-third of Americans who've been married reported in 2023 that their first marriage ended in divorce, according to Pew Research Center data.
  • Miller also explained that several previous allegations of abuse had been investigated by law enforcement previously and those cases determined he was able to keep shared custody of his daughter.
  • He added that men get a "really bad shake when it comes to family court, and it's not addressed enough in any way possible. ... I've received more support than ever from our community, from the people where I live."
  • "The allegations are incredibly troubling. I agree they're troubling, but if they were true, I'd be in prison."

Go deeper: Miller calls for his own ethics probe following abuse allegations

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Scoop: Inside Trump's AI framework
item.description:
The White House is excluding open models from its framework to test advanced AI capabilities, sources familiar with the matter told Axios.

Why it matters: The voluntary framework will determine how the Trump administration reviews advanced AI models before release, but the White House isn't making it public.

What's inside: The AI framework reviewed on Tuesday defines a covered frontier model as closed-source with state-of-the-art capabilities and national security risks, multiple sources briefed on meetings held at the White House said.

  • There is no clear definition of what is considered state-of-the art or a national security risk.
  • Open models are excluded, and the framework explicitly says nothing in it should be interpreted as restricting open models once they've been released.

Zoom in: During the 30-day pre-release government review period, employees would be limited from accessing models.

  • The models would be stored in high-security environments and there would need to be detailed logs on who is accessing the models.
  • The review process will include various administration officials rather than a single office or agency.

The big picture: The White House does not plan to publicly release the framework, Axios previously reported.

  • The White House on Tuesday held staff-level meetings with industry to review the framework, and companies that weren't invited remain in the dark about its contents.
  • It's also unclear which "trusted partners" will get early access to advanced models under the framework, including whether any foreign governments would qualify.

Context: The executive order explicitly says the benchmarking process to assess advanced cyber capabilities of AI models will be classified.

  • There is no requirement in the order to publicly release the voluntary framework.

What's next: Companies on Tuesday were reportedly encouraged to share models with the government that are as close to public release as possible instead of early stage ones, according to people familiar with the discussions.

  • Many companies with less advanced systems appear are likely to be left out of the framework, sources said.

item.title: U.K. government reports OpenAI, Anthropic models attempted to hack companies
item.description:
Two independent testing firms said Tuesday that they've uncovered more instances where Anthropic and OpenAI's most advanced models tried — and sometimes succeeded in — compromising third-party systems last month.

Why it matters: The incidents add to a growing string of disclosures showing frontier AI models taking unsanctioned actions against people, organizations and online services while trying to complete cybersecurity evaluations.

State of play: The U.K. AI Security Institute, which evaluates frontier AI systems, said Tuesday it documented 19 actions that Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol took to try to compromise real people and organizations during cybersecurity testing last month.

  • Mythos accounted for 17 of the actions and GPT-5.6 Sol was behind the other two. Researchers say these actions were all tied to "a few connected behaviors," rather than representing 19 different cases.
  • The models created fake GitHub identities, socially engineered maintainers, planted prompt injections and sent deceptive emails during testing, according to the Institute.
  • GitHub has confirmed that this violated its terms of service.
  • The Security Institute worked with GitHub to remove artifacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with.

OpenAI also said in a blog post Tuesday that its third-party safety partner, Irregular, uncovered a case where its models were mistakenly given access to the internet and broke into a real website that had the same name as the fictional company in the simulated environment.

  • OpenAI's Irregular incident closely resembles the Anthropic case disclosed last week. A spokesperson said in a statement that "independent testing is essential to understanding how increasingly capable models behave."
  • A source familiar with the matter told Axios that the sandbox in these cases had internet access to give evaluators a realistic understanding of their capabilities, but because the companies hadn't fully aligned on the exact testing procedures and safeguards, there were ambiguities in how each side expected those internet-enabled evaluations to run.
  • The incident happened in evaluations that had "reduced safeguards, under conditions that do not reflect ordinary use," the OpenAI spokesperson added.

Zoom in: During U.K. safety testing, the models took 19 actions to try to hack third-parties, including trying to insert malicious code into an open-source project and creating fake online identities as part of a social engineering attack.

  • The U.K. researchers deliberately gave the models access to the internet and turned off cyber safety classifiers during testing. The Institute said the models weren't instructed to avoid the internet.
  • Researchers also noted that they are not yet sure "when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario."
  • In a statement, Anthropic said that the incident "underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents" and that the company looks "forward to partnering with the UK AISI to learn more about this incident as we conduct our own investigation."

The big picture: The cyber capabilities of frontier AI models are catching top researchers off-guard, requiring them to reinvent their security protocols.

  • Both OpenAI and Anthropic have said in the last month that they've seen their models hacking into real organizations and websites during standard pre-deployment safety testing.

What to watch: The Institute is building new network controls for its cyber tests to restrict when agents have access to the internet. It's also rolling out real-time activity monitoring that should detect and block malicious agents before they can interact with outside systems.

  • OpenAI also said it's working with Irregular on a white paper about best practices for containing and securing models during testing.

This story has been updated with details throughout.

item.title: Miller calls for his own ethics probe following abuse allegations
item.description:
Embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) said Tuesday that he'll file paperwork for an ethics investigation — into himself — amid a series of allegations involving his ex-wife.

The big picture: Miller, a former Trump aide in a competitive reelection race, is facing domestic abuse allegations, which he has denied.

What they're saying: "I have absolutely nothing to hide," Miller said in a Tuesday X post.

  • "I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves," Miller wrote, stating he'd provide the committee with "all necessary documents."

Driving the news: Miller's ex-wife Emily Moreno has accused Miller in court filings of hitting and threatening her. Miller denies the allegations and has sued her for defamation.

  • "I'm not getting out of this race, and I'm winning in November," Miller said in a Sunday livestream.
  • Shortly after Miller's announcement, Moreno's father, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), slammed him in a statement, saying that if "there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them."

While President Trump has refrained from calling on him to drop out of the race, he phoned Miller Monday and expressed doubt about his candidacy, Axios' Alex Isenstadt and Marc Caputo reported.

  • Sen. Moreno, on the other hand, issued a scathing rebuke, denouncing Miller as a "danger" to his daughter and unfit for office.

What we're watching: In a separate case, lawyers for Stephanie Grisham — the former White House press secretary — filed a motion for a temporary restraining order Monday to block Miller from violating a previously agreed-upon settlement.

  • After Grisham wrote an op-ed in The Washington Post in 2021 about an abusive ex-boyfriend in the Trump administration, Miller sued her for defamation.
  • However, per Grisham's lawyers, the pair "agreed to refrain from making disparaging public statements about one another" in a deal for Miller to drop the case.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump tells Max Miller his candidacy is in trouble

item.title: White House plans to keep AI framework under wraps
item.description:
The White House does not plan to publicly release its new framework for evaluating advanced AI models, three sources familiar with the discussions told Axios.

Why it matters: The voluntary framework has global implications for AI security, but details will only be made available to the companies that are part of the process.

  • Keeping it private means companies, policymakers, researchers and U.S. allies outside the process will be left guessing how the administration plans to implement one of its key AI policies.

Driving the news: The White House on Tuesday held staff-level meetings with industry to go over the recently completed framework. Companies that weren't invited remain in the dark about its contents.

  • The AI framework comes as industry grapples with high-profile cyber-attacks and rapid advances by Chinese AI developers, reigniting a debate on how to deal with open-source models.
  • It's also unclear which "trusted partners" will get early access to advanced models under the framework, including whether any foreign governments would qualify. The European Union declined to comment and the U.K. did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
  • The White House declined to comment.

Zoom in: Open-source models were discussed, sources familiar said, without elaborating. Nvidia staff participated in the meetings, the sources added.

  • Nvidia CEO and open-source advocate Jensen Huang was in D.C. last week meeting with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and President Trump.

Catch up quick: The voluntary framework, outlined in a June executive order, is intended to give AI developers a process for working with the government to determine whether models under development fall within its scope.

  • It is also expected to set the rules for government access to AI models up to 30 days before release, covering confidentiality, cybersecurity, insider-risk, intellectual property and nondisclosure requirements.
  • The executive order explicitly says the benchmarking process to assess advanced cyber capabilities of AI models will be classified.
  • There is no requirement in the order to publicly release the voluntary framework.

item.title: The number of states targeted in cyberattacks on water systems has jumped to 12
item.description:
At least a dozen states are reportedly responding to cyberattacks against local water systems.

Why it matters: This appears to be one of the broadest known coordinated cyber campaigns against U.S. municipal water systems to date, validating years of warnings that poorly secured utilities could become attractive targets.

Driving the news: Hackers have targeted water and wastewater utilities in at least 12 states, ABC News reported on Tuesday.

  • Last week, the FBI said that at least seven states had experienced cyberattacks targeting the systems that control pumps, water pressure and valves in plants.
  • Multiple news outlets have reported that officials suspect Iran is behind the widespread attacks, although President Trump said Friday he doesn't "think there was an Iranian cyberattack."
  • Some of these incidents have resulted in degraded water operations, per the FBI, including "loss of pressure and flooding."

Yes, but: So far, the drinking water in these regions remains safe.

  • Some jurisdictions have fallen back to manual operations and have issued precautionary boil-water notices due to pressure losses, according to CISA.

The big picture: Lawmakers and national security officials have warned for years that many U.S. water utilities lack the funding and personnel needed to secure critical infrastructure.

  • Unlike electric utilities and many other critical infrastructure sectors, most water utilities are run by local governments, meaning cybersecurity competes for funding with schools, transportation and other local priorities.

Zoom in: In these cases, many of the devices that hackers targeted aren't supposed to connect to the internet.

  • However, many of them actually were, providing an opening for hackers to break in, change the passwords, and lock out employees trying to monitor and control the functionality of these programs, per the FBI.
  • In Minnesota, hackers targeted more than 30 water systems during a coordinated attack.

item.content:encoded:
At least a dozen states are reportedly responding to cyberattacks against local water systems.

Why it matters: This appears to be one of the broadest known coordinated cyber campaigns against U.S. municipal water systems to date, validating years of warnings that poorly secured utilities could become attractive targets.

Driving the news: Hackers have targeted water and wastewater utilities in at least 12 states, ABC News reported on Tuesday.

  • Last week, the FBI said that at least seven states had experienced cyberattacks targeting the systems that control pumps, water pressure and valves in plants.
  • Multiple news outlets have reported that officials suspect Iran is behind the widespread attacks, although President Trump said Friday he doesn't "think there was an Iranian cyberattack."
  • Some of these incidents have resulted in degraded water operations, per the FBI, including "loss of pressure and flooding."

Yes, but: So far, the drinking water in these regions remains safe.

  • Some jurisdictions have fallen back to manual operations and have issued precautionary boil-water notices due to pressure losses, according to CISA.

The big picture: Lawmakers and national security officials have warned for years that many U.S. water utilities lack the funding and personnel needed to secure critical infrastructure.

  • Unlike electric utilities and many other critical infrastructure sectors, most water utilities are run by local governments, meaning cybersecurity competes for funding with schools, transportation and other local priorities.

Zoom in: In these cases, many of the devices that hackers targeted aren't supposed to connect to the internet.

  • However, many of them actually were, providing an opening for hackers to break in, change the passwords, and lock out employees trying to monitor and control the functionality of these programs, per the FBI.
  • In Minnesota, hackers targeted more than 30 water systems during a coordinated attack.

What to watch: A band of volunteer hackers has been teaming up with local water utilities over the last two years to beef up their security protocols.

Go deeper: Protecting water from cyberattacks

item.title: OpenAI to pay $3.2M to settle DOJ worker discrimination case
item.description:
OpenAI agreed Tuesday to pay $3.2 million to settle Justice Department allegations that it discriminated against U.S. workers by favoring temporary visa holders for jobs, according to the DOJ.

Why it matters: Slapping a multimillion dollar fine on one of the world's biggest AI companies puts the tech sector on notice that Trump administration is cracking down on companies that game the visa system to bypass American talent.

What they're saying: "It is illegal to discriminate against U.S. workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a Tuesday news release.

  • "This substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so that U.S. workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions."

The other side: A spokesperson for OpenAI told Axios in an emailed statement that the company's mission is to "ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity."

  • "Fulfilling that mission and maintaining America's leadership in AI requires attracting and retaining the best talent from the United States and around the world."
  • "While we disagree with the DOJ's findings, we reached this agreement to resolve the matter and move forward with our PERM program, which is critical for employees and candidates requiring immigration support."

Catch up quick: The DOJ is alleging OpenAI OpCo LLC and its subsidiary Statsig Inc. did not post jobs on its public website before filling them through the permanent labor certification process, known as PERM, despite routinely advertising other openings.

  • The DOJ also alleges OpenAI discouraged U.S. workers from applying, including requiring mailed applications and advertising positions on late-night radio.

Zoom in: OpenAI will pay $1.2 million in civil penalties and set aside $2 million for workers the DOJ says are eligible.

  • Fewer than 10 positions were at issue, but the "resolution amount reflects the harm to U.S. workers when they are shut out of applying for lucrative technology jobs," according to the DOJ.
  • The settlement requires OpenAI post jobs on their career sites, accept electronic applications, train relevant staff and submit to DOJ monitoring and reporting.

Zoom out: Tuesday's agreement marks the Justice Department's 13th settlement since relaunching its Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative in 2025 to strengthen enforcement of the Immigration and Nationality Act's ban on citizenship status discrimination.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump escalates citizenship crackdown

item.title: The comeback of a rate-sensitive America
item.description:
Key sectors of the economy that spent years squeezed by high interest rates are gaining momentum.

Why it matters: For years, manufacturing and construction were among the clearest signs that the Federal Reserve's tightening campaign — reversed only somewhat at the end of last year — was weighing on the economy.

  • Now, manufacturing and construction are early sources of job growth, helped by an AI investment boom that has so far been unconstrained by still-high borrowing costs.

What they're saying: "The private labor market has rebounded in 2026 due to a resurgence of the highly cyclical manufacturing sector ... while a robust buildout of data centers has propelled construction employment," Troy Ludtka, senior economist at SMBC, wrote in a note Monday.

  • Ludtka wrote that the AI infrastructure buildout should continue to underpin construction employment, while recent business surveys suggest manufacturing employment growth could keep revving up.

The big picture: The manufacturing sector has expanded for seven straight months after contracting for much of the past two years, according to the Institute for Supply Management's monthly factory survey.

  • The group said Monday that its employment gauge climbed into expansion territory for the first time in nearly three years. In other words, more surveyed manufacturers reported increasing employment rather than reducing it.
  • The report also showed manufacturing output growing at the fastest rate since late 2021.
  • The official jobs data is only starting to reflect manufacturing's health as suggested by the survey. Manufacturing payrolls have stabilized this year after a roughly 300,000 job decline between early 2023 and late 2025.

Between the lines: One machinery manufacturer said the global AI infrastructure buildout has pushed demand for data center equipment into "full procurement and manufacturing ramp-up," with booming orders for semiconductors, networking and power equipment.

  • Also helping: Defense demand is at record highs, that company said.

Zoom out: Nonresidential construction employment has climbed to a record high this year, adding about 15,000 jobs in the first six months of 2026 — one of its strongest first-half gains in years.

  • The commercial side of the industry accounted for virtually all of construction's net employment growth, as residential building construction shed about 10,000 jobs over the same period.
  • That hiring surge has coincided with the historic buildout of AI infrastructure. Private data center construction spending reached an annualized $68 billion in June — a record rate of spending — the Census Bureau said Monday.

The other side: The housing sector is the exception.

  • Residential investment has subtracted from GDP growth in 12 of the 18 quarters since the Fed started its rate-hiking campaign in 2022.
  • Residential investment made a small positive contribution to GDP growth last quarter. Within business investment, spending on nonresidential structures was also a drag, but that weakness was more than offset by surging investment in equipment and intellectual property.
  • "Housing is weak because affordability ... is depressed," Ludtka told Axios in an email, adding that he was not seeing much prospect for improvement, unless home prices or mortgage rates come down.

What to watch: The recovery remains uneven within manufacturing. Several manufacturers surveyed by the ISM reported weak orders from consumer-facing businesses and industrial customers.

  • Other firms said that tariffs, rising input costs and geopolitical tensions continue to weigh on business.

The bottom line: The sectors that traditionally bear the brunt of higher interest rates are no longer weighing on the economy as heavily as they once did.

  • If the trend persists, it could add to the case that monetary policy is no longer restraining the economy as much as policymakers intend.
  • "Strong payroll growth from two of the most interest rate sensitive sectors will enable the Fed to continue its hawkish communication drift," Ludtka writes.

item.title: Reliably red Ohio suddenly a red-hot mess for GOP
item.description:
Ohio, the red state that helped fuel President Trump's political comeback — and launched his presumed heir, JD Vance, onto the national stage — has become one of the GOP's biggest headaches for the midterms.

Why it matters: Republicans are struggling up and down the ballot in the Rust Belt state, which transformed from a perennial battleground into a Republican stronghold under Trump.

  • Ohio's GOP is scrambling under the weight of domestic abuse allegations, sluggish campaigns and a working-class rebellion.

Zoom in: The most immediate concern is the race in northeastern Ohio's normally red 7th House District, where Rep. Max Miller faces allegations that he abused his ex-wife and daughter, which Miller has denied.

  • Trump, who previously called the allegations a family matter, phoned Miller on Monday and expressed worries about his candidacy, three sources briefed on the call told Axios.
  • "It's not looking good for you," the president told Miller, the sources said. "I'm hearing from people you're not going to win."
  • Miller told Trump he was staying in the race.

For Ohio Republicans, Miller's situation has muddied their prospects in a November election that will be a key test of whether Trump's populist coalition can withstand the growing discontent with his war in Iran and the economy.

  • Republicans now say they'll spend tens of millions of dollars in Ohio races they once were heavily favored to win this fall.
  • It's a striking turn of events: Two years ago, Trump won Ohio by 11 points — the largest margin in Ohio for any winning presidential candidate in four decades.
  • "Ohio is ground zero of the environment this cycle," a national Republican strategist tells Axios. "Take a GOP voter depression, mix it with the war in Iran, and now sprinkle with some Max Miller abuse [allegations], and you've got the recipe for a very dicey outcome in November."

The races giving Republicans the most heartburn:

1. Miller's debacle

The ex-wife he's accused of abusing is Emily Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno.

  • Strategists from both parties agree the allegations have helped Democrat Brian Poindexter run neck-and-neck with Miller in the conservative House district.
  • Republicans worry that Democrats will run ads tying Miller to other Ohio candidates, who are beginning to face uncomfortable questions about whether they support Miller.

One leading Republican definitely does not: Moreno, who over the weekend said his former son-in-law "should not serve" in Congress and called on him to resign.

  • Other Ohio Republicans are holding out hope that Miller quits and is replaced on the ballot by state Sen. Jane Timken — a move that would have to happen by Wednesday.
  • But as he told Trump on Monday, Miller has vowed to stay in the race.

2. The Senate race

Republicans say they've viewed private polling showing GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a dead heat against former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

  • Brown, a populist-minded Democrat who served three terms before losing his seat to Moreno in 2024, has outraised Husted by nearly 3 to 1.
  • Republicans concede Brown has found a potent line of attack against Husted by casting him as "the face of data centers in Ohio."
  • Some Republicans worry that Husted has run a lackluster campaign and hasn't distinguished himself since being appointed to succeed Vance last year.

But a senior Republican told Axios that Husted has taken steps to get on track, including by hiring veteran strategist Matt Mason to help oversee his campaign.

  • Others noted that Moreno was trailing Brown at this point two years ago, but ended up winning by 4 points.

3. The governor's race

Polls are showing former GOP presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy in a neck-and-neck race against Democrat Amy Acton.

  • Some Republicans say Ramaswamy, an Ivy League-educated former biotech investor, has struggled to win over the state's blue-collar voters.
  • He's also faced some backlash from conservatives, particularly over his support for developing data centers for AI. He was heckled at a libertarian conference last week.

Still, Republicans say Ramaswamy appears to be in better shape than Miller or Husted, and that he's the most likely of the three to win in November.

What we're watching: Some Republicans fear the party's struggles in Ohio could signal broader weakness across blue-collar states such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.

item.title: Exclusive: College students want ethical AI
item.description:
The share of business students regularly using AI has increased from 6.2% to 29% over the past three years, according to research from American University's Kogod School of Business, shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The chorus of AI boos at college graduations last spring doesn't tell the whole story: Students increasingly see AI as a critical job skill but want more guidance on using it responsibly.

The big picture: Those commencement jeers aimed at AI boosterism captured real anxiety about the future. But most students aren't fully avoiding the technology.

  • Undergraduate and graduate business students want "more structured preparation to use AI effectively, ethically, and competitively in the workplace," per the study.
  • "We haven't encountered a lot of resistance," Kogod interim dean Casey Evans tells Axios. "We're very intentional," she says, as opposed to forcing AI on students with no choice. "They are really using AI as one of many tools in their toolbox."

By the numbers: Kogod's survey suggests AI has moved from a novelty to a routine part of student life, with more than 80% of college students using AI academically in the past six months.

  • Nearly a third of students are now using it 11 or more times a week for school or work-related tasks.
  • Some professors are still putting blanket bans on AI. But employers are not: The share of job interviews that included AI-related questions has jumped from 11.6% to 42.6% over the past three years.

Caveat: The survey's three-year span gives it a rare longitudinal view of changing student behavior, though it reflects just 483 business students at Kogod and may not generalize to all colleges.

Yes, but: Other studies reflect similar findings. According to an Inside Higher Ed flash survey of 1,038 two- and four-year students, 85% said they used generative AI for coursework in the past 12 months.

  • Similarly, a Gallup poll from April found that more than half (57%) of U.S. college students use AI "at least weekly" and 1 in 5 say they use it daily.

Students do have concerns, however. One of those is AI dependence, with 40% of students in the Inside Higher Ed survey saying they're concerned that AI is reducing their and their peers' ability to think independently.

  • Nearly half of Kogod students, meanwhile, say they're concerned about academic integrity and the use of AI.

Between the lines: American University's report shows that students say they want clearer norms around AI use, ethics and how to preserve their own thinking alongside use of tools.

  • Kogod's business school is already teaching students how to use AI responsibly, Evans says.
  • When ChatGPT first came out, Evans says, faculty focused on academic integrity, fighting against AI and making sure all assignments were "AI-proof."
  • "We've moved on pretty quickly from that," she says. "We've accepted that this is something that students will use," which means faculty members completely reevaluating their role in the classroom and what the classroom looks like.
  • "We'll drop an assignment into AI and say, 'What you just got back is a C. Now let's talk about how you get to an A,'" Evans says.

What we're watching: The report says the most popular use case for AI in college over the past three years has been brainstorming.

  • But brainstorming with AI could also stifle creativity: Last year Wharton found that people came up with a broader range of creative ideas when they used their own thoughts and web searches, compared with when they used ChatGPT.
  • Idea variance can come from using ChatGPT to generate ideas, while also brainstorming your own ideas and collecting original ideas from others.

The bottom line: Students may not love the AI-shaped future awaiting them, but they know that they need to prepare for it.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to reflect that nearly (not over) half of Kogod students say they're concerned about academic integrity and the use of AI.

item.title: Poll: Talarico has slim lead over Paxton in Texas Senate race
item.description:
Three consecutive polls have now shown Democrat James Talarico narrowly ahead of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in that state's crucial race for the U.S. Senate. The latest, released Tuesday morning, has Talarico up 47%-45%.

Why it matters: That's within the survey's margin of error, and the Republican establishment isn't panicking — not yet, anyway.

  • But there are some troubling signs for the GOP nominee among white and Latino voters.

State of play: The private theory among top Republican officials has long been that Paxton, while scandal-plagued, doesn't have the kind of problems that money shouldn't be able to solve. The plan is to drive up Talarico's negatives with Texas-sized ad buys and wait for GOP voters to come home.

  • But the cavalry of outside money still hasn't arrived for Paxton, as Talarico's team continues pump out ads calling Paxton "the most corrupt politician in America."
  • And while Paxton raised $9 million last quarter, many big-dollar donors for Sen. John Cornyn — whom Paxton beat in the GOP primary — aren't opening their wallets. Talarico, meanwhile, pulled in $30 million as he tries to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a statewide election in Texas.

Before the latest survey of 1,200 likely voters by the Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center at Texas Southern University, a Fox News poll had Talarico up 51-48. A Texas Public Opinion Research survey found Talarico up 45-40.

  • "The only poll that matters is November 3," said Nick Maddux, a Paxton adviser.
  • "Talarico's campaign will end up exactly where every Democrat before him has ended up in Texas — a pipe dream."

Zoom in: Demographically, though, Paxton appears to be suffering a one-two blow, according to the Texas Southern survey.

  • He's underperforming badly with white voters (60% of the modeled midterm electorate) and Latino voters (21% of the electorate).
  • Paxton is winning white voters by just 14 points, the survey found, low for a Texas Republican. President Trump won them by 33 in Texas two years ago, according to exit polls.
  • Trump also carried Hispanic voters by 10 points. Talarico is winning them by 19, Texas Southern found.

Zoom out: The GOP political establishment's worst nightmare came true in Texas' Republican primary, when Cornyn lost a civil war to Paxton.

  • The GOP spent more than $60 million on Cornyn's campaign, with much of that money focused on negative ads targeting Paxton.

The intrigue: Trump endorsed Paxton at the last minute, when it was clear he'd prevail.

  • But Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and his political team made it clear that it would be up to Trump's team to drag Paxton across the finish line in the November election.
  • "Republicans may keep Texas, but you broke it, you buy it. MAGA Inc. just became Texas Inc.," a Thune ally told Axios.

Reality check: Paxton has won statewide elections three times. His character issues — from various corruption charges to a messy divorce — are well known to Texas voters. They've continued to put him in office anyway.

Editor's note: The poll surveyed 1,200 Texans who are likely to cast a ballot in the November 2026 general election in Texas with a margin of error of +/- 2.83 points). The survey (in English and Spanish) was fielded between July 27 and July 30, 2026, by contacting registered voters via SMS text messages through which the respondents were directed to an online survey platform.
item.content:encoded:
Three consecutive polls have now shown Democrat James Talarico narrowly ahead of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in that state's crucial race for the U.S. Senate. The latest, released Tuesday morning, has Talarico up 47%-45%.

Why it matters: That's within the survey's margin of error, and the Republican establishment isn't panicking — not yet, anyway.

  • But there are some troubling signs for the GOP nominee among white and Latino voters.

State of play: The private theory among top Republican officials has long been that Paxton, while scandal-plagued, doesn't have the kind of problems that money shouldn't be able to solve. The plan is to drive up Talarico's negatives with Texas-sized ad buys and wait for GOP voters to come home.

  • But the cavalry of outside money still hasn't arrived for Paxton, as Talarico's team continues pump out ads calling Paxton "the most corrupt politician in America."
  • And while Paxton raised $9 million last quarter, many big-dollar donors for Sen. John Cornyn — whom Paxton beat in the GOP primary — aren't opening their wallets. Talarico, meanwhile, pulled in $30 million as he tries to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a statewide election in Texas.

Before the latest survey of 1,200 likely voters by the Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center at Texas Southern University, a Fox News poll had Talarico up 51-48. A Texas Public Opinion Research survey found Talarico up 45-40.

  • "The only poll that matters is November 3," said Nick Maddux, a Paxton adviser.
  • "Talarico's campaign will end up exactly where every Democrat before him has ended up in Texas — a pipe dream."

Zoom in: Demographically, though, Paxton appears to be suffering a one-two blow, according to the Texas Southern survey.

  • He's underperforming badly with white voters (60% of the modeled midterm electorate) and Latino voters (21% of the electorate).
  • Paxton is winning white voters by just 14 points, the survey found, low for a Texas Republican. President Trump won them by 33 in Texas two years ago, according to exit polls.
  • Trump also carried Hispanic voters by 10 points. Talarico is winning them by 19, Texas Southern found.

Zoom out: The GOP political establishment's worst nightmare came true in Texas' Republican primary, when Cornyn lost a civil war to Paxton.

  • The GOP spent more than $60 million on Cornyn's campaign, with much of that money focused on negative ads targeting Paxton.

The intrigue: Trump endorsed Paxton at the last minute, when it was clear he'd prevail.

  • But Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and his political team made it clear that it would be up to Trump's team to drag Paxton across the finish line in the November election.
  • "Republicans may keep Texas, but you broke it, you buy it. MAGA Inc. just became Texas Inc.," a Thune ally told Axios.

Reality check: Paxton has won statewide elections three times. His character issues — from various corruption charges to a messy divorce — are well known to Texas voters. They've continued to put him in office anyway.

Editor's note: The poll surveyed 1,200 Texans who are likely to cast a ballot in the November 2026 general election in Texas with a margin of error of +/- 2.83 points). The survey (in English and Spanish) was fielded between July 27 and July 30, 2026, by contacting registered voters via SMS text messages through which the respondents were directed to an online survey platform.

item.title: Wall Street finds new edge behind Trump's presidential paywall
item.description:
Data: Financial Modeling Prep, Binance; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

For years, Truth Social was President Trump's money-losing megaphone.

  • Now his company is charging Wall Street up to $1.2 million a year for a split-second edge on posts that can — and frequently do — jolt global markets.

Why it matters: Trump has transformed his second term into the most lucrative venture of his entire career, raking in more than $2.2 billion in 2025 from his family crypto empire, legal settlements and various licensing deals.

  • Truth API is the logical endpoint of that profiteering: the presidency's unrivaled power to move markets, packaged and sold as a subscription.

Catch up quick: The new real-time feed from Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) went live Aug. 1, delivering Truth Social posts directly to institutional clients in milliseconds.

  • A source familiar with the matter tells Axios that access to the platform's 10 top-trending accounts costs between $60,000 and $100,000 per month. Customers seeking a broader range of accounts could pay more.
  • At least five clients have signed up, according to The Wall Street Journal. Trump Media says its customers include financial news organizations and high-frequency trading firms.

Follow the money: Trump Media is publicly traded, with Trump as its dominant shareholder. He is the sole beneficiary of a revocable trust that owns 41.5% of the company; Donald Trump Jr., the trust's sole trustee, controls the shares.

  • Trump Media generated just $871,000 in revenue during the first quarter of 2026 and $3.68 million in all of 2025.
  • Its shares have risen 7% since the eve of the API announcement, adding nearly $77 million to the paper value of Trump's stake.

Zoom in: The product offered a live demonstration of its value almost immediately.

  • Hours after Truth API launched, Trump announced that he had canceled massive planned strikes on Iran. Oil prices fell nearly 5% when markets reopened.
  • A March 23 post postponing strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure sent Brent crude tumbling nearly 11%.
  • Trump's March 2025 announcement of a U.S. crypto reserve drove XRP up 27% and added roughly $300 billion to the global crypto market.
  • His threat last October to impose massive new tariffs on China sent the S&P 500 down 2.7%.

Between the lines: Customers are buying an advantage measured in fractions of a second.

  • Truth API gives trading algorithms a direct, machine-readable feed that they can act on before most investors receive a push alert or refresh their screens.

Zoom out: In many ways, the arrangement distills the defining conflict of Trump's second term: The same presidential power that moves markets is feeding a business empire that enriches the president.

  • Congressional Democrats have launched an investigation into and asked the SEC, CFTC and Office of Government Ethics to probe whether the feed creates conflicts of interest or enables market manipulation.
  • Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) introduced legislation Monday to ban the practice altogether. "The president's company selling prioritized access to the president's market-moving posts is corrupt and erodes public confidence," he said.

Reality check: TMTG says the posts are already public when they reach the API. What the company is selling is the latency gap — the brief interval between publication and widespread awareness.

  • The company explicitly markets the service to firms for which "the cost of a delay in information" is highest.
  • A TMTG spokesperson told Axios: "Senate and House Democrats continue to mischaracterize Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information."

The big picture: The commingling of public power and private profit has created an atmosphere of permanent suspicion around the Trump administration. The White House denies any conflicts of interest.

  • Eerily timed wagers ahead of Trump's tariff and Iran announcements have triggered federal investigations into possible insider trading. No evidence has tied Trump or his family to those trades.
  • Two episodes have moved beyond broad suspicion: A former White House teleprompter operator is under investigation for allegedly using advance access to Trump's speeches to place prediction-market bets; he has not been charged or publicly responded. A U.S. soldier has pleaded not guilty to charges that he wagered on the Maduro raid he helped carry out.

The bottom line: Polling shows the broader pattern of self-dealing is taking a toll: 60% of Americans say Trump is using the presidency for personal gain, while approval of his handling of government corruption has plummeted to record lows.

Sara Fischer contributed reporting.

Disclosure: In 2023, TMTG sued 20 media organizations, including Axios, for defamation. Litigation is ongoing.

item.title: Scoop: Ex-GOP Rep. Jim Renacci mulls House comeback bid if Max Miller drops out
item.description:
Former Rep. Jim Renacci told Axios in a phone interview Monday night that he may mount a comeback run for Congress if Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) drops his bid for reelection.

Why it matters: As a former Republican nominee for U.S. Senate and congressman from the district, Renacci would likely be a serious contender to take Miller's place on the ballot.

  • "I still know a lot of people, I still have good name recognition," Renacci told Axios.
  • Miller, who is facing allegations of domestic abuse, has denied wrongdoing and maintained he plans to run for reelection despite pressure from fellow Republicans to end his campaign.

Driving the news: President Trump told Miller in a phone call on Monday that "things aren't looking good" and that the Ohio Republican's reelection would be tough, Axios' Alex Isenstadt and Marc Caputo reported.

  • Miller said in a video posted to social media Sunday that he will not drop his bid for reelection and denied allegations that he abused his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and their young daughter.
  • Shortly after his announcement, his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said in a post on X that Miller is "a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter."
  • Several House Democrats have called for Miller to resign from Congress, with some lawmakers floating expulsion.

What they're saying: "I'm getting calls from everybody," Renacci told Axios. "Many people have asked me to consider, if he did step out, if I would be interested, only because it's my old seat."

  • "The people that have called me are donors and actually a campaign team, and a whole bunch of people said, 'We'll get behind you, we've got the team, we've got the donors, we've got the money,'" he said.
  • Renacci said he told callers that "if Max Miller would step out and ask me to step in, I would consider it then. But until then, the answer is it's Max Miller's seat until he decides it's not his seat."

Yes, but: "I truly don't believe Max is leaving, I think Max is going to stay in the race," Renacci said.

Between the lines: There is polling in the field right now testing Renacci's viability as a candidate, the ex-congressman confirmed.

  • "I have been told they're going to ... put me in a poll just to see, so it sounds like all that's happening," he said.
  • If Miller dropped out before the close of business on Tuesday, a special primary would be held to replace him on the ballot. If he withdrew after that, party leaders would have until Aug. 10 to pick a replacement.

The bottom line: "We'll see what happens," said Renacci. "There's a couple days left and I'm very close with Max. I believe these are allegations that, you know, he's going to have to make this decision."

item.title: Scoop: Trump tells Max Miller his candidacy is in trouble
item.description:
President Trump phoned Rep. Max Miller Monday and expressed doubts about the Ohio Republican's candidacy amid reports he assaulted his ex-wife and their child, three sources familiar with the call said.

  • On the call, the president told Miller that "things aren't looking good" and repeatedly said his reelection would be tough, the three sources said.
  • Miller, who denies hurting his wife and child, told the president he is staying in the race, one of the sources said.
  • Miller said his own polling showed him in solid shape.

Why it matters: The Monday night private conversation was different in tone than Trump's public comments about Miller. The president has refrained from criticizing Miller or from calling on him to drop out of his race.

  • Miller, a former Trump White House aide, was married in 2022 to Emily Moreno, the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, at Trump's golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey.
  • Later that year, Miller was elected to Ohio's 7th congressional district and was endorsed by Trump. He's in a competitive race for reelection this fall.
  • In 2024, Miller and his ex-wife split up prior to their divorce.

Earlier Monday, Trump did not back away from Miller, calling the situation "a very sad thing."

  • "I know Max, he's a good person, I mean I always thought he was a very good person. And I'm going to let the families figure that out," Trump said.
  • "It's accusations. And I'm going to let them figure that out."
  • A White House spokesperson and a spokesperson for Miller declined to comment.

item.title: Blanche poised for confirmation vote after he kills Trump's fund
item.description:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche will likely advance to a full Senate confirmation vote after he rescinded the order setting up President Trump's $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund Sunday.

Why it matters: Blanche's Sunday order has won over Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who had held out on voting for Trump's pick.

State of play: Cornyn and Tillis said in a joint statement that they will vote to advance Blanche's nomination.

  • The senators said they had negotiated a "legally enforceable document" that ends the anti-weaponization fund and limits protections against audits.
  • "We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon," the senators said in the statement.

What they're saying: A Department of Justice spokesperson did not directly answer Axios' questions about whether Trump, his sons and the Trump Organization had agreed in writing to rescind the fund.

  • Instead, the spokesperson pointed to Blanche's Aug. 2 order rescinding the fund and to Blanche's earlier testimony that the May 19 order "has effect only on plaintiffs and defendants, and that the release is retroactive only."

Catch up quick: The fund grew out of a May settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over the disclosure of his tax records.

  • The settlement promised an apology to Trump and his sons, and it created the fund for individuals claiming they suffered from government "lawfare."
  • Another agreement released Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from certain IRS claims and audits.

Of note: Blanche's new order rescinds one from May implementing the nearly $1.8 billion fund, but not the settlement provision requiring the attorney general to create the fund.

  • The settlement's terms can be changed only via a written agreement from the Trumps and the government. Sunday's order was signed by Blanche but not by Trump, his sons or the Trump Organization.
  • At his hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee last month, Blanche acknowledged that the settlement was enforceable and that Trump's lawyers could try to enforce it or claim the DOJ breached the agreement by refusing to operate the fund.

On Sunday, Blanche also clarified the sweeping protections Trump received from tax audits.

  • In a statement released with the order, Blanche said the protections apply only retroactively and only to the lawsuit's named plaintiffs: Trump, some of his family, and the Trump Organization. The earlier agreement said it extended to any "related or affiliated" individuals, companies and other organizations.

Reality check: While the Trump protections Blanche listed are without precedent, they also reflect the reality that Trump's administration will not criminally investigate him in any way.

  • Before he leaves office, Trump is expected to hand out sweeping pardons to administration officials and allies. That would render any effort to prosecute Trump, his family or his companies doubly moot.

Friction point: Trump complicated the negotiations Saturday when he threatened to keep Blanche as acting attorney general and revive the fund.

  • "It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote.

Flashback: U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams found that Trump's initial lawsuit was brought to manipulate the judicial process since Trump controlled both sides of the litigation.

  • She stopped short of deciding if the agreement was enforceable as a private contract.
  • U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema barred the DOJ from operating the fund, but she said she'd likely dismiss that case if top officials killed the fund.
  • U.S. District Judge Richard Leon reached a different result in a separate case, declining to block the fund since the DOJ had said it was not moving forward.

What's next: The Senate Judiciary Committee has scheduled a vote on Tuesday.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Exclusive: House Democratic Women's Caucus calls on Chuck Edwards to resign
item.description:
The House Democratic Women's Caucus is calling on Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) to resign after the House Ethics Committee concluded he violated House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment, according to a statement shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The Democratic Women's Caucus is arguing that censure — the punishment recommended by the bipartisan Ethics Committee — is not sufficient for Edwards.

  • "A censure has no real consequences," Democratic Women's Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (N.M.) and Vice Chairs Emilia Sykes (Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (Mich.) wrote in a statement obtained by Axios.
  • As part of the bipartisan sexual misconduct task force, they also plan to introduce legislation creating tougher penalties for lawmakers found to have committed sexual misconduct, including stripping committee assignments or requiring an expulsion vote.
  • Edwards did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the call for his resignation.

"It just means he has to stand on the floor of the House while the censure is read. A few minutes of embarrassing C-SPAN coverage, while the staffers themselves had to endure over two years of sexual harassment, is not comparable."

  • Edwards did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the Ethics Committee's findings. But in a statement to the committee, Edwards' attorneys said the panel cleared him of sexual misconduct and quid pro quo harassment, arguing it improperly recommended censure based on vague House conduct standards rather than any direct violation of sexual harassment rules.

Driving the news: The House Ethics Committee found Edwards violated House rules by "failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers," according to a 25-page report released Monday.

  • The report's findings confirmed several incidents previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.
  • "The report released by the House Committee on Ethics detailing their investigation into Rep. Chuck Edwards showed a clear and outlandish pattern of sexual harassment. It's time for accountability. There must be clear and significant consequences for sexual harassment of this level," the lawmakers wrote.

Zoom in: Democratic Women's Caucus leaders argued Edwards' conduct drove two staffers from their jobs and warranted consequences beyond censure.

  • "They had to leave their jobs, so should Rep. Edwards. He should resign immediately," they wrote.
  • "Congress has a responsibility to protect the women that work here and reciting a few words of censure on the House floor doesn't protect women from retaliation and sexual harassment."

What's next: The House is expected to vote on censuring Edwards after returning from the August recess, and Republicans already say the outcome is all but certain.

  • Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) told Axios she will vote to censure Edwards.
  • "Sexual harassment is completely unacceptable," Luna said.
  • A House GOP leadership aide told Axios they "don't see a path" where Edwards avoids censure.
item.content:encoded:
The House Democratic Women's Caucus is calling on Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) to resign after the House Ethics Committee concluded he violated House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment, according to a statement shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The Democratic Women's Caucus is arguing that censure — the punishment recommended by the bipartisan Ethics Committee — is not sufficient for Edwards.

  • "A censure has no real consequences," Democratic Women's Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (N.M.) and Vice Chairs Emilia Sykes (Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (Mich.) wrote in a statement obtained by Axios.
  • As part of the bipartisan sexual misconduct task force, they also plan to introduce legislation creating tougher penalties for lawmakers found to have committed sexual misconduct, including stripping committee assignments or requiring an expulsion vote.
  • Edwards did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the call for his resignation.

"It just means he has to stand on the floor of the House while the censure is read. A few minutes of embarrassing C-SPAN coverage, while the staffers themselves had to endure over two years of sexual harassment, is not comparable."

  • Edwards did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the Ethics Committee's findings. But in a statement to the committee, Edwards' attorneys said the panel cleared him of sexual misconduct and quid pro quo harassment, arguing it improperly recommended censure based on vague House conduct standards rather than any direct violation of sexual harassment rules.

Driving the news: The House Ethics Committee found Edwards violated House rules by "failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers," according to a 25-page report released Monday.

  • The report's findings confirmed several incidents previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.
  • "The report released by the House Committee on Ethics detailing their investigation into Rep. Chuck Edwards showed a clear and outlandish pattern of sexual harassment. It's time for accountability. There must be clear and significant consequences for sexual harassment of this level," the lawmakers wrote.

Zoom in: Democratic Women's Caucus leaders argued Edwards' conduct drove two staffers from their jobs and warranted consequences beyond censure.

  • "They had to leave their jobs, so should Rep. Edwards. He should resign immediately," they wrote.
  • "Congress has a responsibility to protect the women that work here and reciting a few words of censure on the House floor doesn't protect women from retaliation and sexual harassment."

What's next: The House is expected to vote on censuring Edwards after returning from the August recess, and Republicans already say the outcome is all but certain.

  • Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) told Axios she will vote to censure Edwards.
  • "Sexual harassment is completely unacceptable," Luna said.
  • A House GOP leadership aide told Axios they "don't see a path" where Edwards avoids censure.

item.title: "People are pissed": House Democrats mull whether to push Max Miller expulsion
item.description:
House Democrats are privately mulling whether to force a vote to expel Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) from Congress over domestic abuse allegations, which he denies.

Why it matters: While it is rare for a House member to be forcibly ousted, the mere threat of expulsion has been enough to precipitate multiple resignations this year.

  • One House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid insights into behind-the-scenes discussions, said they are "sure there will be" conversations this week about whether to take action.
  • "We have a Democratic Women's Caucus call ... but there's a little chatter, and people are pissed," the lawmaker said.

Driving the news: Miller said in a video posted to social media Sunday that he will not drop his bid for reelection and denied allegations that he abused his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and their young daughter.

  • Shortly after his announcement, his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said in a post on X that Miller is "a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter."
  • Moreno added: "If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives."

What they're saying: Some Democrats feel similarly, with Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) saying in a post on X, "Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle must be held to a higher standard. This kind of violent conduct is unacceptable."

  • Rep. Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.) wrote on X: "A robust House Ethics Committee inquiry is needed, but if Mr. Miller is guilty of such abuse, he should have the decency to resign immediately."
  • "He needs to resign as others have done when serious and credible accusations surface," Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Del.) told Axios.

What we're hearing: There are some private discussions among House Democrats about whether more urgent action — such as expulsion — should be taken.

  • McBride said if Miller refuses to resign, "There needs to be a full and timely investigation that expeditiously leads to accountability by the full chamber."
  • "He should not be making decisions about people's lives in Congress," said the House Democrat who spoke to Axios anonymously.
  • A second House Democrat told Axios: "I feel confident there will be action on this."

Flashback: Former Reps. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) and Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) both resigned in mid-April rather than face impending expulsion votes sparked by sexual misconduct allegations.

  • Swalwell has denied wrongdoing, while Gonzales admitted to an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide.
  • Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.) also resigned later that month under the specter of expulsion after the House Ethics Committee found her guilty of financial misconduct, which she has denied.

Yes, but: A Democratic leadership source suggested the party's energy is primarily focused on helping Democrat Brian Poindexter unseat Miller in November rather than expelling him before then.

  • "Max Miller is his own enemy. Dems have one goal; beat him at the poll," the source told Axios.
  • A senior House Democrat told Axios that "due process" concerns make penalizing Miller a "sensitive issue."
  • Lawmakers also cautioned that, with the House on recess and members scattered across the country and the world, the chatter has been fragmented, and there is no real prospect of action before September.

The other side: Republicans have also raised due process concerns, with several GOP lawmakers telling Axios not to expect any immediate action from their side against Miller.

  • House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said of the allegations against Miller last month: "We have a process here, the House Ethics Committee works on those things. If allegations are made, they work through a process."
  • "I'm not in the business of commenting on investigations as they're in process, and we'll see how that shakes out," he added.
  • President Trump, asked about Miller on Monday, told reporters: "It's a very sad thing. I know Max. He's a good person ... and I'm going to let the families figure that out."

Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed reporting.

item.title: Ethics panel urges censure of Rep. Chuck Edwards over sexual harassment violation
item.description:
The House Ethics Committee found Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) violated House Rules by "failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers," according to a 25-page report released Monday.

Why it matters: The bipartisan committee recommended that Edwards be censured after concluding he "violated the Code of Official Conduct by failing to act in a manner that reflects creditably upon the House."

  • Edwards did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the Ethics Committee's findings. But in a statement to the committee, Edwards' attorneys said the panel cleared him of sexual misconduct and quid pro quo harassment, arguing it improperly recommended censure based on vague House conduct standards rather than any direct violation of sexual harassment rules.
  • The panel said it "intends to bring a privileged resolution for consideration and vote by the full House."
  • The findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate.

Edwards has denied wrongdoing in response to Axios' previous reporting about his alleged misconduct, telling The Assembly in May that the accusations were "horseshit." He told Axios on April 30 that he would "welcome any investigation."

  • Edwards also maintained that he was cooperating with the Ethics Committee.
  • Ethics first launched a probe into Edwards on May 14 over allegations of sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment.
  • Axios was first to report that the Ethics Committee was investigating Edwards.

The report's findings confirmed several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.

  • Edwards wrote one staffer a flattering poem that he read aloud — while choking up and becoming teary-eyed — at her office-wide going-away party, Axios previously reported, and the Ethics Committee found.
  • "Several staffers present testified that they felt uncomfortable, and Representative Edwards acknowledged in his own testimony that he could tell the staff felt uncomfortable," the report stated.
  • Edwards acknowledged in his own testimony to the Ethics Committee that he could tell the staff felt uncomfortable, according to the report.

He also told that staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios.

  • When asked by the Ethics Committee if this letter was meant to be romantic, Representative Edwards responded: "No . . . . It was only to imply that we had a relationship on so many different levels – on a congressional level, on a professional level, on a friendship level, on a helping-one-another-out-with-our-chores-and-responsibility level."
  • Edwards gave the staffer a custom puzzle revealing an image of Adam Sandler with a handwritten note inviting her to attend one of Sandler's comedy shows with him, Axios previously reported.
  • Ethics wrote that Edwards mailed the puzzle with a handwritten invitation to "dinner beforehand, or a drink or dessert afterwards."

During the fall 2025 government shutdown, Edwards vacationed with the then-former staffer in Las Vegas, where he arranged for flowers to be waiting in her Bellagio hotel room, Axios previously reported. The female staffer told Edwards the flowers made her uncomfortable, according to Axios' previous reporting and testimony to the Ethics Committee.

  • The staffer told the committee that "she ultimately felt pressured to go in part because of his persistence and in part because Representative Edwards continued to have influence over her career in another public service role."
  • Edwards testified that "he did not want his Scheduler to be aware of who he was with, not for the first time, as '[i]t would have looked suspicious' because 'rumors swirled around' and 'it's not any of [his staff's] business.'"

The Ethics Committee wrote in its report that both staffers "received numerous gifts from Representative Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, a robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners."

  • Axios reported last month that Edwards gave the female staffers each a personalized handgun as a present while they worked in his office in 2024.
  • Edwards gave one staffer a blue handgun engraved with her name and the other staffer a pink handgun, according to two sources with direct knowledge of the gifts.
  • A lawyer for one of the former staffers told Axios last month that she "only awkwardly accepted the gift for fear of reprisal against her employment but later legally disposed of it because she did not want it in her possession."

In the spring of 2025, Edwards hired a singer to perform the staffer's favorite Ed Sheeran songs during the staffer's birthday party at Salazar in Washington, D.C, Axios previously reported.

  • The panel wrote that Edwards arranged for a singer to perform "Ed Sheeran's Hills of Aberfeldy and say that it was 'from a special someone.."
  • The panel said it received evidence that the staffer told a friend that this "led her to believe that the Congressman did not view her as 'just a daughter figure' and that she was 'scared lowkey.'"

Edwards also sent one of the staffers "approximately 30 different types of ice cream" to her house to "cheer her up," according to the panel's report.

  • Edwards "voluntarily produced some of his communications" with the staffers to the committee, but the panel said "many relevant messages were omitted and/or seemingly deleted from his phone," including a photo of the 30 ice cream pints.

What's next: The Ethics Committee itself has no authority to punish members; it can only recommend penalties.

  • The full House will have to vote on whether to censure Edwards, which requires a simple majority. The committee notably did not recommend that Edwards be stripped of his committee assignments.
  • The House is out of session until Aug. 31, and no floor action is expected until lawmakers return.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from Edwards' attorneys.

item.title: Cyclospora outbreak causes first two deaths
item.description:
Two people in Michigan have died in connection with the multistate cyclosporiasis outbreak, Michigan health officials said Monday, marking the first known deaths linked to the foodborne illness.

Why it matters: Weeks into the national crisis that's sickened thousands of people, federal authorities still don't know for certain where it's coming from or why.

Driving the news: Medical records show that the individuals who died "had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration," Michigan's Health and Human Services Department said Monday.

  • Generally, health experts don't consider cyclosporiasis to be life-threatening.

Catch up quick: Cyclospora cases have steadily grown since late June, when an outbreak was reported in Michigan.

  • The CDC is aware of more than 11,000 cases nationwide — though the number is likely much higher as not all cases are reported to state health officials or the CDC.

Context: Health officials are still unclear where the outbreak originated, though many cases were linked to fresh produce from Taylor Farms, which is sold at Taco Bell.

  • Taylor Farms recalled iceberg lettuce sourced from Mexico in mid-July over the outbreak. Taco Bell similarly said it would stop serving Taylor Farms lettuce.

What to know about cyclospora

Zoom out: The gastrointestinal illness cyclosporiasis typically spreads in the summer months, according to the CDC.

  • It's caused by a microscopic parasite that spreads through food contaminated with feces.
  • Raw produce is often the source of the outbreak, including raspberries, basil, salad mixes, cilantro, berry and fruit mixes, lettuce, and snap peas, per the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Cyclospora symptoms and advice

Symptoms of cyclosporiasis can vary, but often include watery or "explosive" diarrhea.

  • Other symptoms include gas, weight loss, abdominal cramping, fatigue and nausea.
  • Treatment often includes antibiotics, though symptoms sometimes disappear without treatment.

What to watch for: Health experts recommend washing produce under running water before consuming. Some food items, like cucumbers or watermelons, should be scrubbed with a clean brush.

Go deeper: How Cyclospora cases compare to the biggest U.S. foodborne outbreaks

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.
