item.title: The message beneath the yen intervention
item.description:
The U.S. and Japanese governments have acted together to try to prop up the value of the yen on global currency markets. The way they did it contains a clue about U.S. goals — and has some worrying implications for global markets.

The big picture: Headline indicators have been steady across global financial markets this summer. Yet there are some signs of strains beneath the surface, particularly in the form of rising long-term borrowing costs at a time of elevated debt worldwide.

  • The U.S. participation in the yen intervention may have been an effort to enable the Japanese to smooth gyrations in their currency without creating more market pressure for Treasury bonds.
  • Japan has intervened in the market for the yen off and on for decades. What is unusual is for the U.S. Treasury Department to have joined the effort, and to do so in a manner that appears designed to prevent selling of Treasuries by the Japanese government.

Catch up quick: The Japanese government has been sweating yen weakness, which makes oil, food and other imports more expensive and creates financial stability risks.

  • Late last week, the Treasury Department winked and nodded about its involvement with currency market intervention, with a social media post from Secretary Scott Bessent speaking of "a strong relationship and close coordination."
  • In a press event at Camp David, with photographers present, Bessent had a pad in front of him with a "to-do" list that read: "Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil."
  • On Monday morning, both governments confirmed the effort. "Friday's coordinated foreign exchange actions countered disorderly yen movements," Bessent wrote on X. "We will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention."

Zoom in: The two governments appear to have used complementary tools. The New York Fed, acting for the Treasury, reportedly sold euros to buy yen.

  • Meanwhile, the Fed's Foreign and International Monetary Authorities (FIMA) Repo Facility gave Japanese authorities a way to borrow dollars against Treasury securities rather than selling those securities outright.
  • In effect, the U.S. Treasury was acting to strengthen the yen-euro exchange rate. It apparently achieved its goal of strengthening the yen on global currency markets, without the Japanese government selling U.S. government debt on a large scale.

Between the lines: Longer-term U.S. borrowing rates have been marching upward in the last few months, with the 30-year Treasury yield touching new post-2007 highs in recent days. (It was around 5.23% at 11:45am Monday.)

  • Other major countries' rates have also been elevated, reflecting global demand for capital to finance large fiscal deficits and the AI buildout. As global investors demand higher rates to finance massive U.S. deficits, the burden of interest costs on U.S. taxpayers is set to soar.
  • There have been nagging worries that rising Japanese interest rates will prompt the end of the global carry trade, in which hedge funds borrow at low rates in yen to buy higher-yielding assets elsewhere. If the Bank of Japan deals with its currency weakness and inflation problem solely through rate hikes, it could accelerate that process.
  • A plausible story for the U.S. currency intervention is that Bessent is seeking to help the Japanese take action on yen weakness without creating new stress for Treasury bonds, though he and the Treasury have emphasized U.S.-Japanese friendship as the rationale.

For the record: A Treasury official tells Axios that the action was a response to the speed and disorderliness of the yen sell-off, and meant to prevent that instability from spreading.

What they're saying: "Markets are treating this as a currency issue, but it's far bigger than that," Nigel Green, CEO of the financial consulting firm deVere Group, wrote in a note.

  • "When two of the world's largest economies step into the market together for the first time in over a decade, they're telling investors something about stress building beneath the surface of the global financial system, not just about an exchange rate."

Courtenay Brown contributed reporting.

  • On Monday morning, both governments confirmed the effort. "Friday's coordinated foreign exchange actions countered disorderly yen movements," Bessent wrote on X. "We will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention."

Zoom in: The two governments appear to have used complementary tools. The New York Fed, acting for the Treasury, reportedly sold euros to buy yen.

  • Meanwhile, the Fed's Foreign and International Monetary Authorities (FIMA) Repo Facility gave Japanese authorities a way to borrow dollars against Treasury securities rather than selling those securities outright.
  • In effect, the U.S. Treasury was acting to strengthen the yen-euro exchange rate. It apparently achieved its goal of strengthening the yen on global currency markets, without the Japanese government selling U.S. government debt on a large scale.

Between the lines: Longer-term U.S. borrowing rates have been marching upward in the last few months, with the 30-year Treasury yield touching new post-2007 highs in recent days. (It was around 5.23% at 11:45am Monday.)

  • Other major countries' rates have also been elevated, reflecting global demand for capital to finance large fiscal deficits and the AI buildout. As global investors demand higher rates to finance massive U.S. deficits, the burden of interest costs on U.S. taxpayers is set to soar.
  • There have been nagging worries that rising Japanese interest rates will prompt the end of the global carry trade, in which hedge funds borrow at low rates in yen to buy higher-yielding assets elsewhere. If the Bank of Japan deals with its currency weakness and inflation problem solely through rate hikes, it could accelerate that process.
  • A plausible story for the U.S. currency intervention is that Bessent is seeking to help the Japanese take action on yen weakness without creating new stress for Treasury bonds, though he and the Treasury have emphasized U.S.-Japanese friendship as the rationale.

For the record: A Treasury official tells Axios that the action was a response to the speed and disorderliness of the yen sell-off, and meant to prevent that instability from spreading.

What they're saying: "Markets are treating this as a currency issue, but it's far bigger than that," Nigel Green, CEO of the financial consulting firm deVere Group, wrote in a note.

  • "When two of the world's largest economies step into the market together for the first time in over a decade, they're telling investors something about stress building beneath the surface of the global financial system, not just about an exchange rate."

Courtenay Brown contributed reporting.

item.title: What happens if the Fed holds fewer policy meetings
item.description:
Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh is reportedly weighing whether the central bank should hold fewer policy meetings each year.

Why it matters: Cutting the Fed's meeting schedule would be the biggest change to the process of monetary policymaking in decades, reducing the procedural burden on staff but giving policymakers fewer routine opportunities to adjust interest rates as the economy changes.

Driving the news: The New York Times reported Friday that Warsh raised the idea of holding fewer meetings to discuss interest rates, citing four people familiar with the matter.

  • Bloomberg later reported that he floated six rate-setting meetings each year, plus two meetings focused on broader economic issues.
  • Any new schedule could be decided before the Fed's September meeting, according to the Times.

Zoom out: Warsh could make the change without congressional approval. The Federal Reserve Act requires the Fed's rate-setting committee to meet at least four times a year.

  • The current eight-meeting schedule has been the norm since the 1980s.
  • Next year's meeting dates, while noted as "tentative," have already been announced on the central bank's website.

Zoom in: Each of the Fed's eight scheduled policy meetings triggers weeks of staff analysis, briefing books and public communications. Fewer meetings would reduce the frequency of that process.

  • It also would be consistent with Warsh's chairmanship so far: His communications strategy has been restrained on public policy guidance and in sharing his own views.
  • The trade-off: If inflation unexpectedly accelerates — or the labor market suddenly weakens — the Fed might have to wait longer to act, unless it calls an unscheduled emergency meeting.

item.title: White House finalizes AI framework behind closed doors
item.description:
The White House said on Monday it met its deadline to establish a voluntary framework for evaluating advanced AI models — but it won't say what the framework contains, who's seen it or when companies will start using it.

Why it matters: The framework is being closely watched beyond the industry players it directly applies to.

  • Policymakers, AI safety advocates, and U.S. allies have been waiting to see what the rules for the most powerful models in the world look like.

What they're saying: "The voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order was complete by the deadline," a White House official said.

  • "Discussions with industry about next steps are underway," the official said, adding that the administration is engaging with "many more" industry partners than just Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
  • Leading up to the deadline, the three labs gave the administration feedback on a draft of the framework.

What's inside: The framework is meant to give AI developers a structure for engaging the government to determine whether models under development would be covered.

  • The framework is supposed to spell out the confidentiality, cybersecurity, insider-risk, intellectual-property protection use and nondisclosure requirements that would apply when the government gets access to models for up to 30 days before they're released.
  • The framework should also include which "trusted partners" will also have early access to models.

Zoom in: The executive order explicitly says the benchmarking process to assess advanced cyber capabilities of AI models will be classified.

  • The threshold for which models are covered under the order is also classified and will only be shared with AI developers and researchers "as appropriate."
  • The order does not similarly designate the voluntary framework as classified, and policymakers and other observers expected to see details.

Between the lines: Companies are seeking clarity early so they know whether models under development are likely to fall under the framework.

  • "Just because things are unclassified that doesn't mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone," the White House official said.

What's next: The White House will hold a staff-level meeting with companies on Tuesday to review the framework, a source familiar said.

item.title: New Yorker: China races to own the industries of the future
item.description:
America has been napping or distracted by trivialities while China is racing toward the future, in part by taking advantage of President Trump's trade, immigration and budget policies.

  • That's the eye-opening reality that Evan Osnos unfurls in a 12-page piece for The New Yorker, "The Future, Made in China."

Why it matters: China could beat the U.S. to the future on a host of fronts, including engineering a cure for cancer.

What it says: "For China, America's retreat comes just as decades of state investment, industrial policy, and diplomatic planning are paying off," Osnos writes.

  • An American executive told him: "People in Washington are worried that biotech is the next E.V.s ... We've scared all of this f*cking talent back to China. If you look at the guys who are doing this, they used to work for Western pharma giants, or they were running a top university department somewhere."
  • In a flex, China now welcomes Western influencers, investors and commentators on "tech tours" that yield "infrastructure porn" and "Chinamaxxing."

Between the lines: Osnos, who lived in Beijing for eight years as a foreign correspondent, returned for 10 days as part of four months of reporting. He says the capital is noticeably quieter than when he left in 2013 — "an awkward serenity to life in the capital of a high-tech, one-party state."

  • "The vehicles, many of which are electric now, move silently through the streets, and in any case the residents have fewer reasons to go out; China has the world's busiest e-commerce market, and there isn't much that can't be delivered on the back of a scooter," he writes.
  • "All day long, people scan each other's QR codes to swap cash on such digital-payment systems as WeChat and Alipay, feeding the algorithms an ever more intricate portrait of their movements and preferences."

The intrigue: The surveillance future is here: Osnos felt constantly watched — because he was, including psychologically. At an AI expo in Beijing, Osnos stood in front of a kiosk that took an emotional X-ray by measuring "micro-gestures" in his face. The results: He possesses 76.67% positive emotion and 23.33% negative emotion, split between fear and rage.

  • The state can use such readings to zero in on potential disruptors. The same manufacturer makes a scan for schools that assigns pupils an alert level of red, yellow or blue.

By the numbers: China produces 70% of the world's drones, electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries and solar cells, the magazine says, and "deploys more industrial robots than the rest of the world combined, and, in medicine, it has surpassed the United States in the number of registered clinical trials."

  • China's shipbuilding capacity is 200 times that of the U.S.

Friction point: China's rulers avoid "overtly antagonizing America, because they believe that, even in decline, it remains uniquely dangerous."

  • But Rush Doshi, China specialist at Georgetown and CFR, says that if the U.S. loses the next wave of industries — AI, biotech and robotics — as it lost on solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles, "it would irreversibly change the balance of power."
  • A think tank at Renmin University of China, in Beijing, published a report called "Thank Trump," which argues that his tariffs, attacks on allies and immigration policies have hastened the "twilight of an empire."

The bottom line: A European diplomat who has attended meetings with Xi Jinping and his advisers told Osnos they're "feeling like the champions of the world."

item.title: Medicaid's work requirement crunch arrives
item.description:
Massive changes to Medicaid eligibility are entering a new phase as states begin implementing new work rules and patients face the first real risk of losing coverage.

The big picture: The crunch period has started for states to get the word out and set up systems for many Medicaid enrollees to report at least 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering or get an exemption.

  • "If that goes wrong, people are going to be really, really upset, and that is a political firestorm that nobody wants," said Matt Salo, a health care consultant and former executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors.

Driving the news: In Nebraska this week, Medicaid enrollees who fail to report their community engagements will start to lose coverage.

  • Reporting requirements are reportedly already causing confusion for Medicaid enrollees in the state, which is the first to implement requirements well ahead of the Jan. 1 national deadline.
  • The state's Medicaid director said about 200 people will lose coverage this week, and each denial is being reviewed multiple times before enrollees are notified, the health policy podcast "Tradeoffs" reported.
  • Projections show as many as 7 million nationwide could lose coverage as a result of work requirements in 2028.

What they're saying: Patients, providers and advocates flooded the administration with tens of thousands of comments last week, urging changes to its directions for how states must implement the work requirements passed by Congress last year.

  • Many raised concerns that the disability and illness exemptions are inadequate.
  • The American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network released new survey results showing that 90% of cancer patients and survivors said they had to miss work, school or volunteering gigs as a result of their illness.
  • Three-quarters said it would be hard to successfully submit paperwork to prove they worked or get an exemption during treatment.

State of play: Providers are getting anxious, too. The rules for state implementation of work requirements will push responsibility for determining medical exemptions onto clinicians, who are already overburdened by paperwork.

  • "Physicians are trained to diagnose and treat medical conditions — not to conduct vocational or occupational assessments regarding an individual's ability to satisfy government work reporting requirements," the American College of Physicians wrote in a comment letter to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
  • ACP noted that many doctors are already no longer seeing Medicaid enrollees because of the administrative burden. The group asked officials to authorize broader categorial exclusions using claims data that already exists, as well as give states flexibility to determine how they figure out medical exemptions.

The other side: "As with all rulemaking, CMS will carefully review and consider all timely submitted comments as part of the rulemaking process and will determine whether any changes are appropriate in future rulemaking," Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard said.

Zoom out: The comments came as a federal judge in Massachusetts declined a request from half of the states to halt the implementation directions.

  • The Democrat-led states' lawsuit against the Trump administration centers on its rules for medical frailty exemptions from work requirements, which the states argue are more restrictive than Congress intended.
  • Other Medicaid enrollees, including parents of young children and the elderly, are exempt from the requirements regardless of their health status.

Reality check: Work requirements are just one pressure point facing state Medicaid programs and their enrollees, said Robin Rudowitz, senior vice president at KFF.

  • The Trump administration is also freezing funds for some state Medicaid programs under suspicion of fraud.
  • Tighter state budgets, financing changes from last summer's legislation and looming midterm elections are creating "a perfect storm," Rudowitz said.
  • "We're all very focused on work requirements and these are huge, big changes for the program," she said. "But that's happening in the context of many other things."

Editor's note: The story has been corrected to reflect that the survey of cancer patients and survivors was by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (not the American Cancer Society).

item.title: How America is adapting to climate extremes
item.description:
Climate adaptation is increasingly moving from planning to real-world action as heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods and hurricanes test communities across the U.S.

Why it matters: Even if greenhouse gas emissions decline, many communities are already facing more frequent or intense climate extremes, prompting officials to invest in infrastructure designed to reduce future damage.

Driving the news: After catastrophic flooding killed more than 130 people in Texas Hill Country last year, newly installed sirens were credited with warning residents during July's floods, which killed three people but avoided a repeat of the 2025 disaster.

  • It's an example of Republican-led states adapting after disaster, said Alice Hill, senior fellow for energy and the environment at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Texas expanded flood-warning systems and floodplain buyouts after the Hill Country floods, while Houston strengthened building codes after Hurricane Harvey.
  • "Building to the last disaster is like preparing for the last war," says Hill, who served as a senior resilience policy official on President Obama's National Security Council.

Between the lines: Hill said "almost all the infrastructure" in the U.S. "was built for a climate that essentially no longer exists."

  • Mikhail Chester, director of the Metis Center for Infrastructure and Sustainable Engineering at Arizona State University, tells Axios that the infrastructure industry is learning that climate hazards "cost more to ignore than to actually start to design for" and that these risks "have become that much more real over the past decade."
  • However, Hill says adaptation is still running behind the scale of the challenge.

The big picture: Rather than rebuilding after every disaster, many states are redesigning infrastructure for the climate threats they face most — from hurricanes in the Southeast to droughts and wildfires in the West.

  • Chester says insurers are helping shape adaptation by pricing climate risk into infrastructure decisions.
  • Hill says insurers have largely focused on limiting their exposure, with only a handful of programs rewarding resilience with lower premiums.

State of play: Since Hurricane Ian, Florida has invested in backup power, stronger building codes and microgrids — small-scale power grids that supply electricity to local areas and can operate independently when the main electric grid fails.

  • Louisiana utilities have hardened substations and strengthened the electric grid after repeated hurricanes.
  • California has expanded wildfire-resistant building standards, underground power lines and drought measures such as water recycling and groundwater recharge.
  • Los Angeles has added cool roofs and urban forestry, while Phoenix has become a national leader in cooling centers and other heat- and drought-adaptation measures.

Zoom in: Some communities are moving ahead despite federal funding constraints and the Trump administration's push to scrub references to climate change from government websites.

  • One example is Babcock Ranch, Florida, where a developer buried power lines, improved storm drainage, and built more wind-resistant homes. The community has since weathered four hurricanes with little damage, Hill says.
  • "We're seeing lots of exciting developments," Hill says. But she warns that "most of our infrastructure is not built for what is coming."

Zoom out: Professional engineering organizations are publishing climate-adaptation standards that states and local governments can adopt.

  • Chester says engineers increasingly recognize the limits of relying solely on concrete channels and pipes, prompting greater use of parks, wetlands and other forms of green infrastructure.

The bottom line: Communities are showing climate adaptation can reduce damage and save lives. The bigger challenge is preparing for the next disaster — not simply rebuilding after the last one.

Go deeper: Sirens put to work as Texas Hill Country again slammed with floods

item.title: Democrats lack a leader right now — and might not get one until 2028
item.description:
You're probably less than 600 days from Democrats having a true leader who can show and shape the party's direction.

Why it matters: Until Super Tuesday — that's March 7, 2028 — or well beyond, Democrats will be leaderless, and likely split between rising socialist energy and more traditional, establishment liberalism.

  • DNC Chair Ken Martin will likely get ousted and leave behind a hot financial mess and cashless dumpster fire.
  • Hakeem Jeffries has a legit shot at rising to speaker, but will lack a big enough majority as well as the instincts and ambition to lead beyond the House.
  • Chuck Schumer's future is fragile. If he doesn't win the majority, he'll get challenged for the top job. Then, he'll be preoccupied with AOC running for his Senate seat and ending his career. Even if she goes for the White House instead, his future at home and as party leader is in doubt.
  • Barack Obama is the only Dem with true national sway — and he's made plain he wants to work things mostly behind the scenes.

This leaves Bernie Sanders as the most powerful kingmaker for '28 given his network and sustained popularity. Advantage: AOC.

The bright side: Dems will be juiced to win back power in '28, knowing a better Senate map awaits and confident voters will want to move beyond Trump's drama.

  • They'll see the path to full control of D.C. thanks to one wild stat: 17 of 22 presidents going back to Teddy Roosevelt took office with full control of government. Clinton, Bush 43, Obama, Trump and Biden all did.

Between the lines: Insane political volatility is the rule, not the exception, of modern elections. This means more regulatory and policy uncertainty, including the rising possibility of socialism among Democrats and sustained Trumpism among Republicans.

What to watch: The 2028 Senate map is the best in a decade for Democrats. Republicans hold 19 of 34 Senate seats that'll be up, including Wisconsin, North Carolina and Ohio.

item.content:encoded:
You're probably less than 600 days from Democrats having a true leader who can show and shape the party's direction.

Why it matters: Until Super Tuesday — that's March 7, 2028 — or well beyond, Democrats will be leaderless, and likely split between rising socialist energy and more traditional, establishment liberalism.

  • DNC Chair Ken Martin will likely get ousted and leave behind a hot financial mess and cashless dumpster fire.
  • Hakeem Jeffries has a legit shot at rising to speaker, but will lack a big enough majority as well as the instincts and ambition to lead beyond the House.
  • Chuck Schumer's future is fragile. If he doesn't win the majority, he'll get challenged for the top job. Then, he'll be preoccupied with AOC running for his Senate seat and ending his career. Even if she goes for the White House instead, his future at home and as party leader is in doubt.
  • Barack Obama is the only Dem with true national sway — and he's made plain he wants to work things mostly behind the scenes.

This leaves Bernie Sanders as the most powerful kingmaker for '28 given his network and sustained popularity. Advantage: AOC.

The bright side: Dems will be juiced to win back power in '28, knowing a better Senate map awaits and confident voters will want to move beyond Trump's drama.

  • They'll see the path to full control of D.C. thanks to one wild stat: 17 of 22 presidents going back to Teddy Roosevelt took office with full control of government. Clinton, Bush 43, Obama, Trump and Biden all did.

Between the lines: Insane political volatility is the rule, not the exception, of modern elections. This means more regulatory and policy uncertainty, including the rising possibility of socialism among Democrats and sustained Trumpism among Republicans.

What to watch: The 2028 Senate map is the best in a decade for Democrats. Republicans hold 19 of 34 Senate seats that'll be up, including Wisconsin, North Carolina and Ohio.

item.title: Energy Dept. draws fire for slow pace of Venezuelan oil deals
item.description:
Nearly eight months after President Trump predicted U.S. companies would "rapidly rebuild Venezuela's dilapidated oil industry" to boost production, no new petroleum deals have been finalized there with American firms.

  • The U.S. Department of Energy is largely to blame, a dozen oil industry professionals, senior U.S. officials and Venezuela insiders tell Axios.

Why it matters: The price of oil is climbing as the Iran war squeezes global supplies, spotlighting the absence of finalized deals in Venezuela — a nation with the highest estimated petroleum reserves on the planet.

  • "We have no new concessions. No new deals. It is absolutely a problem," a senior U.S. official told Axios. "The Energy Department is in charge of this and they have some explaining to do."
  • The Energy Department and its defenders call the criticisms misleading and unfair, and say that new oil deals will be signed in the coming weeks.

Zoom in: Developing oil in Venezuela is challenging because of the legacy of mismanagement and nationalization efforts under its two prior socialist strongmen, Hugo Chavez and Nicolas Maduro.

  • Maduro was ousted by U.S. forces Jan. 3. Six days later, Trump met with oil industry officials and said the U.S. is "going to be making the decision" about which firms would help "rapidly" rebuild in Venezuela.
  • "You're dealing with us directly," Trump said. "You're not dealing with Venezuela at all. We don't want you to deal with Venezuela."

Between the lines: Trump's promise was hampered by two divides — one in his own government; the other in the oil industry.

  • The oil industry is separated between major global firms that move relatively slowly and deliberatively, and smaller independent firms — nicknamed "wildcatters" — known for their speed and higher risk tolerance.
  • The "majors," like Exxon and ConocoPhillips, publicly made clear they were cool to the idea of going back to Venezuela because of all the uncertainty. But several wildcatters were eager to get in.

Trump's administration, meanwhile, is split between MAGA types and regulatory professionals.

  • MAGA loyalists want Washington to heed what Trump said Jan. 9 and force Venezuela's state-run oil company, called PDVSA, to quickly adopt common international industry contracting standards.
  • The more cautious bureaucrats in the Energy Department, who have relatively little international oil-industry experience, advocated for a slower process, working more collaboratively with Caracas.
  • A new complication: Two earthquakes June 28 badly damaged Venezuela. Discontent there is rising.

Friction point: Trump's former top adviser in Venezuela, Mauricio Claver-Carone, accused the Energy Department of favoring the major oil companies over the wildcatters.

  • "Starting January 4th, it should have been carte blanche for all American producers to take risk. That's America First," Claver-Carone told Axios.
  • "Instead, American wildcatters got stuck with onerous conditions and a competitive disadvantage versus the mostly foreign majors that were in bed with Maduro."

Over time, more wildcatters aligned with MAGA and officials at the White House's National Energy Dominance Council. They clashed with the more cautious bureaucrats in the Energy Department.

  • "NEDC was there early advocating for the wildcattters. But Energy is really turf-obsessed. And Energy won. The problem now is that they own this," said one oil industry insider.
  • In recent weeks, State Department officials stepped in to urge Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, to sign more contracts with wildcatters, teeing up deals that could be finalized by month's end.
  • One industry official raised concerns that some of the imminent deals might involve newly formed companies with no track records, no balance sheets and potential links to China or corrupt Caracas insiders.

The other side: Energy Department officials say they've advocated for legitimate U.S. wildcatters and they've worked to improve Venezuela's hydrocarbon law to give U.S. firms more access.

  • "The Energy Department continues to work with Venezuelan officials and American energy companies of all sizes to unleash Venezuela's resource potential, and we are delivering," department spokesperson Ben Dietderich said, adding that both oil production and exports are up to levels "few thought possible."
  • Alex Cranberg, a wildcatter with Colorado-based Aspect Energy, said officials are "drinking from a fire hose" in Caracas, trying to manage the demand and keep scammers out.
  • Bill Armstrong, owner of Texas-based Armstrong Oil & Gas, said the Energy Department and PDVSA officials are "working hard behind the scenes" to reorient the industry.

Behind the scenes: Two other independent companies shared documents with Axios showing that, for months, they asked the Energy Department to force PDVSA to recognize standard international high-risk contracts for oil drilling, but not enough was done.

  • "We're months behind. We'd be lifting oil now if we got half the deference the majors got," one wildcatter told Axios.
  • "The problem isn't that Energy is doing too much in Venezuela — it's that they're doing it for the wrong customers," said a representative of another oil firm. "Put the wildcatters in the fields and production shoots up straight away."

For weeks, White House officials have fielded industry complaints as well as requests that Secretary of State Marco Rubio take over the portfolio from Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

  • Rubio has deferred to the Energy Department's expertise, partly because many firms want the U.S. government to "pick winners and losers" by favoring one company over another.
  • The major companies, meanwhile, are battling to redevelop some of the same fields, according to the Wall Street Journal.

By the numbers: Venezuela produces about 1.2 million barrels of oil today. That's slightly above the 1.1 million barrels daily it was producing before Trump instituted a blockade-like quarantine in November and then seized Maduro to start the year.

  • At its peak, Venezuela produced about 3.4 million barrels daily in 1998. The following year, Chavez took office and oversaw the deterioration of the industry.
  • If the regulatory floodgates had opened on Jan. 4, estimates vary as to how much oil production would increase —from hundreds of barrels daily to hundreds of thousands.

White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said the Energy Department "is ushering in unprecedented investment in Venezuela to restore its energy infrastructure."

  • She added that the department "continues to facilitate productive conversations between oil companies and the Venezuelan government to unleash its abundant resources, which benefits both the American and Venezuelan people."

item.title: U.S. wildfire season exceeds 10-year average as 99 large fires burn
item.description:
Wildfires in Washington and Oregon have forced evacuations, caused power outages, and burned hundreds of thousands of acres as firefighters battle dozens of massive fires across the Pacific Northwest.

Why it matters: The blazes are among 99 active large fires burning across the U.S. as this year's wildfire season exceeds the 10-year average for both the number of fires and the acres burned, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

  • So far this year, 45,835 fires have burned more than 5.2 million acres across the U.S., the NIFC says.

State of play: Washington has 17 active large fires. In the Spokane area, three major blazes — known collectively as the Spokane Complex Fire — have forced some 60,000 people to evacuate, knocked out power to thousands more, and destroyed about 640 structures, officials said Sunday.

  • Gov. Bob Ferguson on Saturday declared a statewide emergency, saying it was "due to our drought conditions, unusually high temperatures and high winds all exacerbating our record-setting wildfires."
  • Oregon has 32 active large fires — the most of any state. Fresh fires ignited Saturday, sparking new evacuation orders.
  • With nearly two months left in the traditional fire season, Oregon set a modern record for acres burned, according to the Statesman Journal and Central Oregon Daily, citing Northwest Coordination Center data.

Zoom out: Idaho and Montana each have seven active large fires, per the NIFC. Minnesota and California each have six, Colorado and Nevada each have five, while Florida and Utah have three apiece. Alaska, Arizona, New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Wyoming each have one.

Between the lines: Climate change is contributing to larger, more frequent wildfires across much of the U.S. West, studies show. It is also increasing the frequency of critical fire weather and driving more extreme fire behavior, making fires harder to contain.

What we're watching: Wildfires and poor air quality are expected to continue across the Pacific Northwest, the Rockies and parts of the Plains, according to the National Weather Service.

  • A red flag warning has been issued for Oregon's southern Willamette Valley from 1-8pm local time Monday, while a fire weather watch has been issued for Tuesday in the western Columbia River Gorge.

Go deeper: The health risks of wildfire smoke and air quality

item.title: Rep. Max Miller not dropping out after domestic abuse allegations
item.description:
Ohio GOP Rep. Max Miller said Sunday he will stay in his reelection race, using a livestream on X to deny allegations he abused his ex-wife and their young daughter.

  • Shortly after his announcement, his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), denounced him as a "danger" to his daughter and unfit for office.

Why it matters: The extraordinary public split between two Trump-aligned Ohio Republicans comes days before the state's deadline to replace Miller on the ballot with a special election — and will only fuel the controversy attached to a seat Democrats are targeting.

What we're watching: A reporter asked President Trump aboard Air Force One Sunday whether he thought Miller should resign following the allegations.

  • "I'm gonna look at it," Trump said. "I mean, so far, it's accusations. I'll be looking at."

What he's saying: "I'm not getting out of this race, and I'm winning in November," Miller said near the end of his livestream.

  • Miller said no court or government agency has substantiated an abuse allegation against him and that he has never faced criminal charges related to the allegations.
  • He said a child-welfare agency deemed two reports that he'd abused his daughter as unsubstantiated. One report recorded an "indicated" finding of physical abuse, meaning investigators saw signs of abuse but lacked sufficient evidence and didn't know who caused it.
  • Miller also denied assaulting his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who had said Miller threw hot water from a skillet and sprayed her with a sink hose during a 2024 argument. He acknowledged spraying her but denied the water was scalding. He said he did not intend to hurt her and called the incident "horseplay."

The other side: Sen. Moreno issued a blistering denunciation shortly after the livestream, saying Miller's behavior had forced him to speak publicly after trying to protect his family's privacy.

  • "He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter," Moreno wrote on X.
  • "If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them," he added. "He should not serve in the House of Representatives."
  • Stefan Mychajliw, a spokesperson for Emily Moreno, called the livestream a "bizarre and lie-filled rant" and accused Miller of using their daughter as a "PR pawn" to save his political career.

Catch up quick: Emily Moreno, who divorced Miller last year, has accused him in court filings of hitting and threatening her. Miller denies the allegations and has sued her for defamation.

  • In addition, Emily Moreno alleged their daughter's collarbone fractured while in her father's care, according to medical records. Miller denied causing the injury and argued the bruising resembled marks from a car-seat strap, per court documents.
  • Police records show prosecutors didn't file charges after concluding there was "insufficient admissible evidence" to present to a grand jury.
  • Miller previously faced abuse allegations from ex-girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, a former Trump White House press secretary. He also denied those claims and sued her for defamation before dropping the case as part of a 2023 settlement.
  • Grisham sued Miller last month, arguing his recent public statements had violated the settlement's nondisparagement and confidentiality terms.

The intrigue: Miller later responded to Sen. Moreno's statement by saying that if his daughter had made similar allegations, he would not have waited two years to act.

  • He accused Sen. Moreno of " speaking out now … to hide from your own media circus."
  • Miller also posted a curated packet of court, police and child-welfare records, along with selected screenshots and recordings. The documents repeatedly name his daughter and provide a home address for his ex-wife.
  • Some records omit pages.

Between the lines: Miller faces Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, in Ohio's 7th congressional district outside of Cleveland.

  • Voters in the district backed President Trump by 11 percentage points in 2024, 10 points in 2020 and 12 points in 2016.

What to watch: Wednesday is Ohio's deadline to trigger a special election to replace Miller on the ballot. Republicans could still fill a vacancy through a party committee but would have to certify a replacement by Aug. 10.

  • If he withdraws after Aug. 10, Republicans can't replace Miller.
  • One name floated by prominent Republicans as a potential replacement is former GOP state chair Jane Timken, a state senator with the capacity to self-fund a campaign.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details throughout.

item.title: Exclusive: Newsom shows fundraising muscle for state parties
item.description:
Gavin Newsom is quietly banking a lot of goodwill among party organizers and elected officials in states — particularly in the South — that will be key in the midterms and the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

  • Newsom has raised more than $1.7 million for critical state parties and their legislative committees so far this two-year cycle, according to data reviewed by Axios.

Why it matters: State party leaders told Axios that the California governor has raised more for them than any other prominent Democrat and potential White House rival.

  • Newsom's ability to raise the money almost entirely through his email list shows that he could be a formidable grassroots fundraiser in a White House run.

Driving the news: Newsom raised the most for the Democratic Party in South Carolina, which is expected to host the first contest in the 2028 primary.

  • Jay Parmley, executive director of the state party, confirmed that Newsom raised over $300,000 for the state party from grassroots fundraising.
  • "He's raised the most. [New Jersey Sen.] Cory Booker has pitched in, and there are others," he said, also mentioning Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly. "But Newsom's is a bigger amount," Parmley told Axios.
  • "He rose to the occasion when we were all facing redistricting challenges," he said. "It's allowed us to increase our staffing and it came at really crucial times for us when we were recruiting candidates to run for the state legislature."

Raymond Buckley, chair of the party in New Hampshire, praised Newsom for his "phenomenal fundraising assistance."

  • Newsom raised over $220,000 for the party and over $56,000 for the New Hampshire Senate Democratic Caucus this cycle.

Molly Forgey, senior adviser for the Nevada Democratic Party, said that "Newsom's fundraising emails have raised more for the Nevada state party than anyone else."

  • Forgey noted that other potential 2028 candidates have raised significant money for ballot initiatives and other Nevada campaigns.

By the numbers: Newsom raised money for 14 state parties from more than 74,000 donors.

  • Besides South Carolina and New Hampshire, the states were New Jersey ($158,063) Michigan ($154,000), Nevada ($117,455), North Carolina ($121,971), Louisiana ($113,615), Florida ($99,808), Tennessee ($95,259), Alabama ($94,865), Virginia ($77,831), Minnesota ($63,836), Georgia ($43,843) and Texas ($30,351).

Like many other potential 2028 candidates, Newsom also raised money for Democrats in key 2026 races such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff; former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who's running for Georgia governor, and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola, who's running for Senate.

  • Newsom's Campaign for Democracy group and its affiliated committees had over $14 million cash on hand at the end of June, according to the Federal Election Commission.

Zoom out: Other Democrats eyeing a presidential run also have given cash to state parties and the national Democratic Party apparatus.

  • Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg recently donated $5,000 to each state party through his outside group Win the Era.
  • Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has for years donated millions of his personal billions to progressive ballot initiatives and candidates, including this cycle.
  • Kelly raised $400,000 for Ossoff and to help other Democrats in key races, the New York Times reported.

Zoom in: Since Newsom faced a recall election in 2021, he and his team have been steadily building an online small-dollar fundraising apparatus.

  • Key architects of Newsom's fundraising machine are Sydney Hibbs and Tim Tagaris, who was instrumental in building Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' small-dollar fundraising operation in the 2020 presidential campaign, when Sanders didn't hold any traditional high-dollar fundraisers and yet out-raised most of his opponents.

State party leaders have been impressed by the amount of money a single email from Newsom's team can raise.

  • "His email list is platinum," said South Carolina's Parmley. "We're an early [primary] state but I have watched him from afar, raising money all across the country. There's no one in politics raising money like Gavin Newsom."

  • Newsom has raised more than $1.7 million for critical state parties and their legislative committees so far this two-year cycle, according to data reviewed by Axios.

Why it matters: State party leaders told Axios that the California governor has raised more for them than any other prominent Democrat and potential White House rival.

  • Newsom's ability to raise the money almost entirely through his email list shows that he could be a formidable grassroots fundraiser in a White House run.

Driving the news: Newsom raised the most for the Democratic Party in South Carolina, which is expected to host the first contest in the 2028 primary.

  • Jay Parmley, executive director of the state party, confirmed that Newsom raised over $300,000 for the state party from grassroots fundraising.
  • "He's raised the most. [New Jersey Sen.] Cory Booker has pitched in, and there are others," he said, also mentioning Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly. "But Newsom's is a bigger amount," Parmley told Axios.
  • "He rose to the occasion when we were all facing redistricting challenges," he said. "It's allowed us to increase our staffing and it came at really crucial times for us when we were recruiting candidates to run for the state legislature."

Raymond Buckley, chair of the party in New Hampshire, praised Newsom for his "phenomenal fundraising assistance."

  • Newsom raised over $220,000 for the party and over $56,000 for the New Hampshire Senate Democratic Caucus this cycle.

Molly Forgey, senior adviser for the Nevada Democratic Party, said that "Newsom's fundraising emails have raised more for the Nevada state party than anyone else."

  • Forgey noted that other potential 2028 candidates have raised significant money for ballot initiatives and other Nevada campaigns.

By the numbers: Newsom raised money for 14 state parties from more than 74,000 donors.

  • Besides South Carolina and New Hampshire, the states were New Jersey ($158,063) Michigan ($154,000), Nevada ($117,455), North Carolina ($121,971), Louisiana ($113,615), Florida ($99,808), Tennessee ($95,259), Alabama ($94,865), Virginia ($77,831), Minnesota ($63,836), Georgia ($43,843) and Texas ($30,351).

Like many other potential 2028 candidates, Newsom also raised money for Democrats in key 2026 races such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff; former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who's running for Georgia governor, and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola, who's running for Senate.

  • Newsom's Campaign for Democracy group and its affiliated committees had over $14 million cash on hand at the end of June, according to the Federal Election Commission.

Zoom out: Other Democrats eyeing a presidential run also have given cash to state parties and the national Democratic Party apparatus.

  • Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg recently donated $5,000 to each state party through his outside group Win the Era.
  • Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has for years donated millions of his personal billions to progressive ballot initiatives and candidates, including this cycle.
  • Kelly raised $400,000 for Ossoff and to help other Democrats in key races, the New York Times reported.

Zoom in: Since Newsom faced a recall election in 2021, he and his team have been steadily building an online small-dollar fundraising apparatus.

  • Key architects of Newsom's fundraising machine are Sydney Hibbs and Tim Tagaris, who was instrumental in building Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' small-dollar fundraising operation in the 2020 presidential campaign, when Sanders didn't hold any traditional high-dollar fundraisers and yet out-raised most of his opponents.

State party leaders have been impressed by the amount of money a single email from Newsom's team can raise.

  • "His email list is platinum," said South Carolina's Parmley. "We're an early [primary] state but I have watched him from afar, raising money all across the country. There's no one in politics raising money like Gavin Newsom."

item.title: Ossoff: The next thing, or "Great White Hype" for Dems?
item.description:
Jon Ossoff is having a moment. But some Democratic insiders are questioning whether he's the real deal — or if a few slickly produced videos are making him look like more of a political juggernaut than he is.

Why it matters: The Georgia senator, 39, has catapulted into the 2028 conversation by making liberals on social media swoon over his viral clips of high-energy rallies and sharp takedowns of President Trump and Republicans.

  • Our conversations with Democratic strategists in Georgia and beyond — as well as aides to his potential 2028 rivals — revealed a mix of respect for Ossoff's digital skills and skepticism that they add up to a serious presidential campaign-in-waiting.
  • One Georgia Democrat went so far as to compare Ossoff's rise to "The Great White Hype," a 1996 comedy about a Black boxing promoter who recruits an amateur white boxer to draw more money and attention.

Zoom in: The strategists said Ossoff has earned much of the buzz that's building around him.

  • But they worry that his core team of advisers is too insular and that the nationwide chatter about him has gone to his head, even as he focuses on his Senate reelection campaign this year. Among their critiques:

1. He hasn't yet proved he can be nimble in the modern media environment.

  • The Democrats point out that Ossoff's videos have largely featured him delivering prepared speeches — not talking off the cuff.
  • Those who know Ossoff personally say he's studious to the point of being self-serious, that his prep sessions regularly go extra long, and that he isn't one for small talk.
  • Ossoff also hasn't been as active on the podcast circuit as other potential 2028 presidential contenders. He's stuck to more predictable environments such as interviews with the liberal network MS Now or brief interactions with TMZ.

Kyle Tharp, a progressive operative who writes a newsletter about digital media, told us that Ossoff's team is "very talented" but that their "perfectly choreographed clips" are a big part of "fueling the Jon Ossoff 2028 hype machine."

  • The question, he said, is whether Ossoff can have "more unscripted moments and long-form conversations."

2. Ossoff got where he is by riding Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock's coattails.

  • Ossoff flipped a Senate seat in 2021 in a key presidential battleground, and could be on the verge of another win: Polls show him leading Republican Rep. Mike Collins by up to double digits.
  • But some Democratic strategists argue that Warnock pulled Ossoff across the finish line when they ran in the 2021 runoff election. Warnock, a senior pastor at Atlanta's Ebenezer Baptist Church, where Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. once preached, outperformed Ossoff in the runoff — then held on to his seat in 2022 despite political headwinds during the Biden administration.

"Ossoff didn't get here alone," Rich McDaniel, a Georgia-based Democratic strategist and an architect of former Alabama Sen. Doug Jones' 2017 victory, told Axios.

  • "Many would argue it was Warnock who carried him in 2020, not the other way around, and that's the ghost that will always follow him," McDaniel added. "What should worry Georgia Democrats more is the pattern underneath it: Black voters build the coattails every cycle, then get left behind when it's time to hire the strategists and control the resources. Ossoff has a chance to break that cycle instead of repeat it."
  • Warnock is widely seen as another potential 2028 presidential candidate, and he's taken more steps toward a run than Ossoff — writing a book and campaigning in Nevada, an expected early primary state in 2028.

3. Some strategists think the progressive left's crush on Ossoff may be short-lived.

  • Many Democrats have been searching for a presidential candidate in 2028 who can bridge the party's moderate and progressive wings.
  • Some think that could be Ossoff, pointing to positive comments made by left-wing voices such as Hasan Piker and Mehdi Hasan.
  • But other Dems think the love affair will be over once progressives learn Ossoff has opposed policies such as Medicare for All and abolishing ICE.

Ossoff, who's Jewish, also has sometimes struggled to navigate the fraught politics surrounding Israel.

  • Ossoff built credibility among some progressives when he voted for proposals by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders aimed at limiting arm sales to the country. But Jewish Democrats in Georgia expressed feelings of betrayal over his votes in November 2024.
  • Five months later, Ossoff voted against two of Sanders' amendments that would have blocked $8.8 billion in arms sales to Israel.
  • Ossoff also could face attacks from the left over his ownership of bonds in the state of Israel totaling $1,001 to $15,000, which were noted in his 2024 financial disclosure.

One Democratic strategist who's worked on Georgia races told us "the thing that worries me most" is that Ossoff could follow the trajectory of Mallory McMorrow, a Michigan Senate candidate who tried and failed to woo both flanks of the party in this year's primary.

  • "Most people thought McMorrow would come out of Michigan because she had both the centrist appeal and the progressive appeal," the strategist said. "But she wasn't able to find a lane."

What they're saying: An Ossoff spokesperson pointed to previous comments the senator has made denying he's eyeing a presidential bid.

  • "I have zero interest in running for president in 2028," he told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution this summer.
  • "2028 fantasy football is a distraction from the urgent task at hand: midterm victory."

Yes, but: Many past presidential candidates initially denied they were interested in running — and Ossoff could endanger his Senate reelection campaign if he overtly moved toward a 2028 bid now.

What's next: Ossoff's political future will hinge on whether he defeats Collins — and by how much he'd run up the score in a victory.

  • If Ossoff wipes the floor with Collins, Ossoff could finally prove he doesn't need Warnock's coattails.

item.title: The pre-Trump GOP is coming for Vance ahead of 2028
item.description:
The Wall Street Journal opinion page tried to stop Donald Trump a decade ago and again in 2024. Now, the standard-bearer of traditional conservatism is making an early case against his presumed heir.

Why it matters: Vice President JD Vance has the inside track for Trump's endorsement. But there's a not-insignificant GOP faction that never embraced Trump's overhaul of the party — and is already arguing against handing the reins to Vance.

Driving the news: In a series of recent columns, Journal opinion writers have ripped Vance for being too self-promoting, too eager to court Tucker Carlson, and too thin-skinned.

  • The columns were written by Kimberley Strassel and Allysia Finley — both members of the Journal's editorial board. One of the pieces was an unsigned editorial.

The main arguments:

1. Vance is putting his ambitions ahead of governing.

  • As congressional Republicans have tried to pass an agenda that might avoid an election wipeout in November, Strassel wrote, "Mr. Vance is promoting a book." She was referring to Vance's recent media tour to promote his just-published bestseller, "Communion."
  • "What experienced legislators wish the newbie Mr. Vance would understand is that his résumé polishing is doing no one any favors — not the party, not the president, not even himself."

2. His personality rankles.

  • Strassel wrote a follow-up piece after Vance's fans came after her for her earlier column. "One answer [for the aggressive response] is simply that Mr. Vance is a sensitive bunny," she wrote. "But the other answer is that Mr. Vance knows his 'national conservative' ambitions for the GOP aren't landing."

3. He's naive.

  • Finley and an unsigned WSJ editorial zeroed in on Vance's defense of the memorandum of understanding with Iran that quickly unraveled, as well as his claims that the Iranian regime had turned over a new leaf.
  • "We promise that wasn't Mr. Obama or John Kerry speaking," the editorial board wrote dismissively.

4. He cozies up to Carlson.

  • "Mr. Vance has spent the Trump presidency trying to curry favor with Mr. Carlson as part of laying the ground for a 2028 presidential run," Finley wrote, calling the VP's diplomatic outreach to Carlson "bizarre given how the pundit has made common cause with the far left" on Israel.

Between the lines: Vance's critics fall into three interlocking circles.

  1. Pro-Israel conservatives.
  2. Traditional Republicans who, broadly speaking, want to turn the clock back to the pre-Trump revolution in their party.
  3. The Murdoch empire. Rupert Murdoch clashed repeatedly with Trump — during the president's first campaign, and again when he staged a comeback early in the 2024 cycle — before bending to him both times. The owner of the Journal and Fox News also lobbied Trump not to pick Vance for VP.

The three groups converge on the paper's opinion page.

The other side: Vance's army of supporters fired back at Strassel over her assertion that he's been AWOL from Congress. According to Vance's office, he's been there over two dozen times since he became vice president. (His office declined to comment beyond that.)

  • Vance was doing his job defending the MOU that his boss signed, his allies say. They note he didn't respond to the column that led Strassel to call him thin-skinned — his supporters did.
  • More broadly, the allies say the Journal is fighting the last war — clinging to a vision of conservatism the Republican Party has left behind.
  • If anything, his backers say, the paper's criticism helps Vance politically — showing he's in tune with the party's grassroots and not heeding the old guard.

"No one in Vance's orbit is concerned or surprised about being attacked by the literal beating heart of the pre-Trump GOP establishment," a top Vance ally told Axios. "When the Wall Street Journal ed board hits him, it only sends the exact signal to our base that we want. ... These guys are doing our work for us."

  • A Trump administration official who also served in the first term called the editorial board "a relic of a bygone era. Their globalist screeds haven't carried weight among GOP voters in the real world for years and only appeal to a small group of establishment never-Trumpers in D.C."

Context: The GOP has changed drastically over the past decade. The parts of the party pining for a return to pre-Trump policies may be deluding themselves.

  • Vance mirrors Trump on trade and immigration — the two issues at the center of Trump's overhaul of the party, and on which the Journal is most at odds with the administration.
  • Elite opinion matters less than it once did, as Trump's rise showed.

Zoom out: The backdrop for all of this is that many Vance-skeptical Republicans want Secretary of State Marco Rubio (who's been adamant he won't run) instead.

  • Axios reported last month that Ken Griffin — one of the most prolific donors in GOP politics — said he'd back Rubio over Vance in a primary.
  • "Regime Change," the bestseller by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, revealed that when Trump asked Murdoch for his opinion on Vance and Rubio (with the two sitting awkwardly nearby), the News Corp. boss said Vance "has the potential to be great" but that Rubio is "brilliant."
  • Strassel was explicit in making the contrast: "Mr. Vance might follow the example of a current prospective rival. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is pursuing the [former VP Mike] Pence model: Put your head down, do the work, let the results speak," she wrote in April.

The bottom line: Trump vanquished the Bush-era GOP, but he's a unique breed. Assuming Vance runs, he'll have to show he can do the same.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional context.

item.title: "Growing pressure" as Nancy Guthrie search passes six months
item.description:
Six months after Nancy Guthrie was taken against her will from her Arizona home in the middle of the night, there are no suspects or major leads and the case seems to be stalled, a source close to the investigation tells me.

  • "There is plenty of blame to go around, but there is growing pressure to solve this case," the source said. "This case has struck a chord — people are watching very closely. This can't go on for another six months."

Savannah Guthrie, the "Today" show co-host and Nancy's daughter, wrote on Instagram on Saturday: "This is our beautiful Mom. Six months ago, someone took her out of her bed in the dead of night. We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair ever since."

  • "We are begging for help," Savannah added. "We are desperate. We need someone to come forward. Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. ... Perhaps they are angry or upset for being in this situation. There is a way out - to tell what you know. You can do so anonymously. The reward is available. There is a way to end this situation and do the right thing. ... We will never stop looking for answers - and we will never stop looking for the light. ... Please. Bring her home. 💛"

Between the lines: A troubling but almost overlooked aspect of the case is that the perpetrator has evaded detection in one of the highest-profile and most closely watched cases in decades. Can shrewd criminals, using the latest technology, now outfox law enforcement?

Behind the scenes: A Wall Street Journal investigation published Saturday night uncovers "a trail of missteps" and finger-pointing between the FBI and Pima County Sheriff's Department.

  • "County sheriff's deputies at first minimized the importance of dried blood found on Nancy's front porch," the Journal found.
  • "They failed to seal off the property with police tape to protect sensitive crime-scene evidence, allowing reporters, livestreamers, and Amazon and pizza delivery drivers entry to the porch. Investigators spent precious hours deciding whether Nancy was kidnapped or lost. A search-and-rescue plane sat grounded until dusk, awaiting a deputy trained to operate its sophisticated surveillance system."

The FBI told the Journal: "The state is the lead in this investigation ... The FBI has met every assistance request asked of us, even when requests came late."

  • The FBI now may face pressure to take a bigger role, the source told me.

item.title: Trump's final act begins
item.description:
President Trump doesn't much care if Republicans lose the House and/or the Senate in the midterms this fall.

  • Yes, he'd prefer a big win, but he seems indifferent to the election and the possibility of endless Democratic investigations of his family, wealth and policies, his closest advisers tell us.
  • A big reason: Trump knows he'll emerge just as strong, or even stronger, heading into his final two years, at least among Republicans.

Why it matters: Trump will enjoy a more pro-Trump Republican Congress, win or lose; gleefully play '28 kingmaker and further test the boundaries of presidential power beyond legislating, his preferred method anyway. He'll use pardons to protect his people, the advisers say.

The big picture: Trump is not a share-the-stage, pass-the-torch, groom-your-successor kind of guy. Instead, he'll exploit his leverage:

  1. A more MAGA Senate. Almost all of his critics will be gone through defeat or retirement. The incoming class is very Trumpy. If they keep the Senate, Trump loyalists like Mike Lee (Utah), Ron Johnson (Wis.) and Rick Scott (Fla.) will chair committees.
  2. A more MAGA House. Trump already serves as de facto speaker, but his few outspoken GOP critics — Thomas Massie (Ky.) and Marjorie Taylor Greene (Ga.) — will be gone, replaced by members who won because of him.
  3. A '28 kingmaker. Trump's firm hold on the base means he will dictate the GOP's nominee AND shape their message. He wants a Vance-Rubio ticket and will likely get it if his mind doesn't change. Imagine any '28 hopeful, especially Marco Rubio or JD Vance, trying to break with the boss while working for the boss.
  4. Cashing in. Trump will use levers of power to keep raising money to expand his clout beyond the presidency. "He likes the fact that when he tells someone, 'Give me money,' they give him money," an adviser told us. Another chimed in: Trump will relish, in perpetuity, having Republicans beg for his endorsement: "You're as powerful as your bank account says you are."

Three dramas to watch post-November:

  1. Trump will flirt with running again in '28 until the bitter end, but it's all about PR and keeping Vance and Rubio in their place.
  2. As potential outside-the-walls competition in '28, the White House is watching Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) and Sen. Josh Hawley (Mo.).
  3. Most importantly: A constitutional clash over congressional oversight, among the last and most vital powers lawmakers hold dear. What happens if Trump orders his entire administration, family and friends to just ignore Congress?

📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

item.title: AI's manifesto war
item.description:
Silicon Valley's AI moguls are flooding Washington with competing blueprints for superintelligence, clashing over a defining question: Does safety come from spreading powerful AI or containing it?

Why it matters: Their fight will shape who gets access to the best models, how America competes with China, and whether the government can slow the race in an emergency.

Driving the news: Alarming developments, seemingly by the day, have turned the manifestos from thought exercises into an urgent policy battle.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic both disclosed that their advanced models went rogue and broke into external systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
  • Kimi K3 delivered a double shock: The Chinese model not only reached frontier-level performance, but did so with open weights that anyone can download, modify and deploy.

The big picture: The shocks have sharpened the stakes for the flurry of manifestos dropping across Silicon Valley.

  • Each mogul's post offers a different theory of the danger — and a different prescription for containing it.

The manifesto map:

  • July 14 — Set the standards: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis proposed an industry-funded, federally overseen "Frontier AI Standards Body" to test models before release. Voluntary reviews could eventually harden into binding rules governing access to the most powerful systems.
  • July 24 — Open the defense: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued that open models give American developers and cybersecurity defenders more tools, and rallied Meta, Microsoft, Google and OpenAI to sign a letter, "Open Weights and American AI Leadership," supporting the open AI ecosystem.
  • July 27 — Gate the danger: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for "mandatory safety testing," and tighter controls on the chips and distillation techniques helping China develop powerful open-weight models. He stopped short of supporting a blanket ban.
  • July 28 — Spread access: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg cast broadly available "personal superintelligence" as a safeguard against a future controlled by a handful of companies and governments.
  • July 28 — Build the brake: More than 1,200 frontier-lab employees signed "Pacing the Frontier," a petition asking Washington to create international tools for deliberately slowing development if AI begins advancing beyond human control.

Reality check: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is trying to occupy both sides of the divide. His lab backs investment in the open AI stack, despite selling closed models.

  • Altman told reporters on Capitol Hill on Wednesday that OpenAI researchers helped shape the pacing letter.
  • We're told Altman has talked with the White House about building the necessary tools to "pace" AI development, preserving the government's option to do so if needed in the future. Altman wants the tools and decisions in the hands of government, not any one company, so it's managed via democratic processes.
  • Altman's No. 1 topic in administration and White House meetings was previewing the capabilities of the company's most powerful AI yet — Astra, the next major ChatGPT model family, as yet unreleased. OpenAI said Saturday that an internal version of Astra was behind research leaps in 10 major open mathematical problems in "high-dimensional geometry, coding theory, arithmetic circuit complexity, group theory, operator algebras, quantum complexity, lattice cryptography and extremal combinatorics."

Zoom out: The open-weight paradox runs through every manifesto.

  • Open weights can spread innovation, strengthen cyber defenders and prevent a few companies from monopolizing AI.
  • But as models gain stronger cyber and autonomous capabilities, the same openness can place dangerous tools beyond any company's ability to monitor, restrict or recall.

Between the lines: These are competing theories of danger.

  • Huang and Zuckerberg fear that concentrated control will weaken America and empower a small group of gatekeepers.
  • Amodei and the pacing coalition fear that powerful capabilities will spread faster than companies or governments can contain them.
  • Altman is trying to preserve the advantages of openness while building an emergency brake for the frontier.

What to watch: The Trump administration is close to issuing a formal process ("voluntary framework") for reviewing cutting-edge AI systems. The manifestos aim to influence which risks that process should prioritize, and whose rules Washington should adopt.

item.title: Trump cancels Iran attack, citing progress in negotiations
item.description:
President Trump said Saturday night that he has called off a potential attack on Iran due to progress in negotiations between the two nations.

The big picture: There had been indications from some U.S. officials that an attack on Iran's infrastructure was possible, all in an effort to get the Iranians to agree to the U.S.' terms in ceasefire negotiations.

What they're saying: "I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," the president wrote on his Truth Social account.

  • Trump added that Iran and "other Middle Eastern Countries" had asked the U.S. to hold off on attacking "in that the perimeters of a deal had been agreed to."
  • "This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat," he wrote.

Zoom out: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Trump spoke on Saturday, with MBS expressing concern over the strike plans, Axios' Barak Ravid and Marc Caputo reported hours before the president's social media post.

  • Other regional powers, including Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Pakistan, have also pressed the U.S. and Iran to de-escalate.

Between the lines: An attack on Iran's infrastructure and energy sites would escalate the war that the president has repeatedly pressed pause on in order to negotiate with Iran, only for strikes to resume when diplomacy appeared stalled.

  • Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned off the U.S. and Israel — which was expected to join the U.S. in a large-scale strike — from any further action.
  • "Any hostile action by the U.S. or Israel — or participation or cooperation by regional countries in such actions — would be met with a decisive and proportionate response from Iran's powerful armed forces," Araghchi said to Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister Prince Faisal Bin Farhan Bin Abdullah Al Saud, per a post on Araghchi's Telegram channel.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Scoop: Saudi crown prince raises concerns over Trump's plans for massive Iran strikes
item.description:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke to President Trump on Saturday and expressed concern over his plans for massive new strikes against Iran, according to two U.S. officials and a third source with knowledge of the call.

Why it matters: Trump is seriously considering attacking Iranian energy targets in the coming days in response to Iran's missile strike on a U.S. base in Jordan and its continued disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. He has yet to issue final orders.

The big picture: Such an attack could lead to an unprecedented escalation in the five-month war, which has repeatedly paused as Trump opened the door to negotiations — only to resume when those diplomatic efforts failed.

Zoom in: Iran has threatened to retaliate by launching attacks against energy and infrastructure facilities in Israel and the Gulf countries.

  • "The Saudis expressed concern and asked for clarity about the plan of action," one U.S. official told Axios.
  • A second source with knowledge of the call said MBS urged Trump to de-escalate and refrain from launching the strikes.
  • The White House and the Saudi embassy in Washington declined to comment.

Catch up quick: Trump met Wednesday with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, known as KBS.

  • The meeting was added to the Saudi minister's itinerary after he met with Vice President Vance and told him that Saudi Arabia favored de-escalation with Iran, a source familiar with the matter said.
  • The message came despite this week's joint U.S.-Saudi strike against pro-Iranian militias in Iraq.
  • The source said the meetings were intended to convey MBS' views on the Iran war and the broader regional situation.

Between the lines: Saudi Arabia is one of Washington's most important allies in the region. Despite periods of tension over the past five months, Riyadh has influenced Trump's Iran policy at several critical moments since the war began.

Driving the news: Other regional powers, including Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Pakistan, are also pressing the U.S. and Iran to de-escalate.

  • Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke Saturday with Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who has served as a key mediator between Washington and Tehran.
  • Araghchi also spoke with the foreign ministers of Turkey and Saudi Arabia about the prospect of U.S. strikes.
  • "Any hostile action by the U.S. or Israel — or participation or cooperation by regional countries in such actions — would be met with a decisive and proportionate response from Iran's powerful armed forces," Araghchi told his Saudi counterpart, according to a statement on his Telegram channel.

What to watch: Qatari mediators held separate talks Saturday with Araghchi, White House envoy Steve Witkoff and Omani officials in an effort to secure an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

  • The talks made progress, a source with knowledge of the discussions said, though it remains unclear whether that will be enough to defuse the crisis.

item.title: Tillis says Blanche won't be confirmed as AG amid Trump fund fight
item.description:
Sen. Thom Tillis said Saturday morning that new comments by President Trump about his "anti-weaponization" fund mean that attorney general nominee Todd Blanche won't be confirmed by the Senate next week.

Why it matters: Tillis's comment escalates the fight between the White House and holdout Senate Republicans over whether Trump's fund — for people he considers victims of political persecution — is dead or not.

What they're saying: "Despite comments as late as yesterday that the fund is dead, President Trump clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against," Tillis (R-N.C.) posted to X.

  • "It's unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday."

For the record: The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post when asked for comment.

The big picture: The "anti-weaponization" fund has been the red line for Tillis and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas). The lawmakers have refused to vote for Blanche until the DOJ put into writing that aspects of the deal aren't moving forward.

  • Tillis and Cornyn both sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee, and at least one of their votes is needed to advance Blanche's nomination to a confirmation vote before the entire Senate.

Yes, but: Earlier Saturday, Trump posted to Truth Social that if Tillis and Cornyn weren't going to vote for Blanche, he would maintain Blanche as acting attorney general and revive a bill to establish the fund.

  • "Todd Blanche was a voice of reason! It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," Trump said.

Background: The president on Thursday floated withdrawing Blanche's name and keeping him on in an acting capacity until Cornyn and Tillis leave the Senate this January.

  • But on Friday, Trump said Blanche should be "immediately approved," a call seconded by members of his administration.

The bottom line: The fights over Blanche, the fund, and Trump's influence over Senate Republicans are converging, with no clear end in sight.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details throughout.
