item.title: DeepSeek's new bargain model accelerates AI's race to zero
item.description:
Data: Axios research; Chart: Sara Wise/Axios

Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released a powerful new coding model Friday that charges pennies for vast amounts of code — the latest sign that some of the smartest software on Earth is rapidly becoming a commodity.

Why it matters: Tech giants are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into the computing infrastructure powering the AI revolution. Yet the intelligence that infrastructure produces is getting cheaper by the week.

Zoom in: DeepSeek is the same Chinese startup that ignited a market meltdown last January by showing it could build a world-class AI model with far fewer resources than its U.S. rivals.

  • Its newest model, V4 Flash, performs close to the level of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8, one of the industry's most capable systems, on tests of complex coding and autonomous software tasks.
  • On Arena.ai's crowdsourced leaderboard for front-end coding, V4 Flash debuted ahead of Opus 4.8 — while delivering the best performance for its price of any model in its class.
  • The price gap is staggering: DeepSeek charges about 28 cents for the same amount of output that costs $25 on Opus 4.8 — a 99% discount.

Zoom out: With Chinese models like Kimi K3 bearing down on the U.S. market, July ushered in a full-scale price war across the AI landscape.

  • OpenAI slashed the price of GPT-5.6 Luna — its fastest, cheapest model for high-volume tasks — by 80% on Thursday, only three weeks after its launch.
  • Google released three new Gemini "flash" models all focused on efficiency.
  • SpaceXAI released Grok 4.5, Elon Musk's most capable model yet for coding, research and autonomous tasks, at the same price OpenAI originally charged for Luna before this week's cut.
  • Meta quietly reversed course on its longtime embrace of open weights with Muse Spark 1.1, a closed-source model priced aggressively for developers.

The other side: Anthropic remains the clearest holdout, keeping its top-tier Claude models at premium pricing and betting that developers will pay extra for safety and precision.

Between the lines: When a product becomes a commodity, buyers care less about who made it and more about what it costs. Think electricity or gasoline: Few people know which power plant supplied their home or which refinery produced the fuel in their tank.

  • AI is heading that way fast. As the performance gap between top-tier models is shrinking, many AI applications no longer depend on a single provider, giving buyers more leverage to shop on price.
  • "At some point, the next model doesn't matter to you," says Zack Kass, OpenAI's former head of go-to-market and a global AI adviser. He calls the phenomenon "diminishing model returns."

What to watch: That could create a lucrative market for "intelligent routers," Vinesh Sukumar, Qualcomm's vice president of AI product management, told Axios.

  • Those systems would automatically choose the best model for each task based on capability, speed and price — further weakening the power of any one lab to command a premium.
  • For frontier AI labs, that could pose an existential challenge: Spending tens of billions to build a slightly smarter model may buy only a temporary lead, without creating lasting pricing power.

Reality check: Falling prices do not necessarily doom the frontier labs if cheaper AI unleashes vastly more demand.

  • OpenAI is betting that companies will use its models so extensively that enormous volume can compensate for thinner margins.
  • "We will have so much usage of our models that we do not need to be a gigantically high-margin business to be able to afford model training," CEO Sam Altman said on the "Invest Like the Best" podcast.

The bottom line: The U.S. and China are both racing to make intelligence abundant. Now someone has to prove abundance can still be profitable.

  • Meta quietly reversed course on its longtime embrace of open weights with Muse Spark 1.1, a closed-source model priced aggressively for developers.

The other side: Anthropic remains the clearest holdout, keeping its top-tier Claude models at premium pricing and betting that developers will pay extra for safety and precision.

Between the lines: When a product becomes a commodity, buyers care less about who made it and more about what it costs. Think electricity or gasoline: Few people know which power plant supplied their home or which refinery produced the fuel in their tank.

  • AI is heading that way fast. As the performance gap between top-tier models is shrinking, many AI applications no longer depend on a single provider, giving buyers more leverage to shop on price.
  • "At some point, the next model doesn't matter to you," says Zack Kass, OpenAI's former head of go-to-market and a global AI adviser. He calls the phenomenon "diminishing model returns."

What to watch: That could create a lucrative market for "intelligent routers," Vinesh Sukumar, Qualcomm's vice president of AI product management, told Axios.

  • Those systems would automatically choose the best model for each task based on capability, speed and price — further weakening the power of any one lab to command a premium.
  • For frontier AI labs, that could pose an existential challenge: Spending tens of billions to build a slightly smarter model may buy only a temporary lead, without creating lasting pricing power.

Reality check: Falling prices do not necessarily doom the frontier labs if cheaper AI unleashes vastly more demand.

  • OpenAI is betting that companies will use its models so extensively that enormous volume can compensate for thinner margins.
  • "We will have so much usage of our models that we do not need to be a gigantically high-margin business to be able to afford model training," CEO Sam Altman said on the "Invest Like the Best" podcast.

The bottom line: The U.S. and China are both racing to make intelligence abundant. Now someone has to prove abundance can still be profitable.

item.title: Trump considering strikes on Iranian energy targets within days
item.description:
President Trump is seriously considering launching attacks against energy targets in Iran in the next few days, but hasn't given final orders to do it, a U.S. official told Axios on Friday.

Why it matters: A new U.S. bombing campaign in Iran against energy and infrastructure targets would be aimed at trying to get the Iranians to agree to the United States' terms in ongoing ceasefire negotiations.

  • The strikes could also involve the Israeli military for the first time in many weeks, and such an escalation would likely lead to Iranian missile attacks on Israel.
  • CBS News and the Wall Street Journal first reported about the potential strikes.

What they're saying: At the start of Friday's Cabinet meeting, Trump alluded to the potential attack, saying: "Well, we'll be hitting them very hard and, you know, at some point they're going to say, we just can't take it anymore."

  • He added that the more the U.S. conducts strikes, the weaker the Iranians get "and then they peter out."
  • "As President Trump said at his Cabinet meeting today, the United States will win, and Iran will not have a nuclear weapon under his watch," White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt told Axios.

Between the lines: A U.S. official said the Iranians have been "very aggressive" in recent days.

  • Some U.S. officials were stunned by how much the Iranians were willing to escalate.
  • After their surprise missile attack against a U.S. base in Jordan on Wednesday, the Iranians launched additional attacks against U.S. forces in the region, a U.S. official said, declining to give more details.
  • The Iranians also attacked commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday.
  • President Trump threatened several days ago that any new attacks on ships would be answered with U.S. strikes on power plants and bridges in Iran, including in Tehran.

The other side: Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, quoted a senior security official saying that U.S. strikes on Iranian infrastructure targets would be "an act of madness."

  • "We have prepared a broad response plan that includes strikes against the Zionist regime's critical infrastructure and U.S. energy infrastructure in the region, and we are fully prepared to carry it out," the Iranian security official told Tasnim.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Trump's comments reignite Blanche confirmation fight
item.description:
The Trump administration is still pushing lawmakers to confirm acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, even as President Trump defends the "anti-weaponization" fund holding Blanche's confirmation hostage.

The big picture: The "anti-weaponization" fund has been the red line for Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.). The lawmakers have refused to vote for Blanche until the DOJ put into writing that aspects of the deal aren't moving forward.

  • Trump said Friday the fund is dead, but he didn't seem happy about it.
  • "I wish it weren't [dead]," Trump said of the fund. He added that he wanted to see people who "were horribly treated, horribly abused" by the government be compensated.

Friction point: Tillis seemed to take issue with Trump defending the fund on Truth Social, retweeting a screenshot of the president's words on Friday and writing that Trump had "made it clear" that the fund "is still alive."

  • "I will continue working in good faith to put an end [to] this legal and political albatross and prevent any potential misallocation of taxpayer dollars," Tillis wrote, adding that Blanche had been forthright in discussions.

Earlier Friday, the president went after Cornyn, and said he would "always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure."

  • Cornyn also re-shared a post Friday that said it "does not sound like citizen Trump has agreed to end the Fund."

Catch up quick: The president on Thursday floated withdrawing Blanche's name and keeping him on in an acting capacity until Cornyn and Tillis leave the Senate this January.

  • But on Friday, Trump said Blanche should be "immediately approved," a call seconded by members of his administration.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in a Friday post that the Senate shouldn't go on recess until Blanche is confirmed.
  • The White House also released a demand to confirm Blanche "without delay" on its website Friday with a list of endorsements from law enforcement groups, former DOJ officials and members of Congress, among others.

What we're watching: While the battle over Blanche plays out in Washington, attorneys for the president said Friday that they'd appeal a Miami-based federal judge's order that blasted the extraordinary deal to drop the IRS suit against his own government.

  • U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams wrote in her scathing order earlier this month that the lawsuit had been a "bad faith" means to an end and blocked the parties from referring to the settlement in any official proceedings — but Trump is still fighting.

Go deeper: The major controversies stalling Todd Blanche's attorney general nomination

item.title: Fed rates dissenters make their case for higher rates
item.description:
Inflation has been too high for too long, and the Federal Reserve should not count on it fading without further action.

  • That is the argument from the three Fed officials who dissented from the decision led by chairman Kevin Warsh to leave interest rates unchanged this week, preferring instead to raise them.

Why it matters: Together, the dissents lay out a blueprint for the Fed's hawkish wing, arguing that repeated supply shocks paired with resilient demand have made inflation too persistent to fade on its own without tighter monetary policy.

  • The question in the months ahead is whether that argument persuades more policymakers, especially if inflation remains stubborn.
  • It is worth watching whether they turn out to have momentum persuading other voting members of the Fed's policy committee in the weeks ahead.

What they're saying: "I increasingly believe that monetary policy does have an important role to play in addressing a series of successive supply shocks that might lead to entrenched higher inflation," Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari said in a statement Friday morning.

  • In a separate statement, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said she is "not confident" that inflation will return to the Fed's 2% target on its own.

The big picture: The three dissenters broke with the majority by voting for a quarter-point rate increase. They emphasized different concerns but reached the same conclusion: Rates are not holding back the economy enough to bring down inflation.

  • "Labor, consumption and financial market conditions indicate that monetary policy is not restraining the economy," Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan wrote in a statement. "Without any policy restraint, inflation will likely continue to trend above target until there's an unanticipated shock."

Between the lines: Kashkari said the Fed should usually look through temporary supply shocks.

  • But he said that after years of disruptions — from the pandemic and Ukraine to tariffs and the Middle East conflict — inflation risks becoming entrenched.
  • Kashkari invoked a parallel to the 1970s as a reminder that successive shocks can ultimately require tighter policy.

Zoom in: Kashkari pointed to one additional factor — the "massive investment in data centers," which he said has added a new demand element to the inflation outlook.

  • Hammack said she was seeing "inflationary pressures coming from the demand side of the economy, as well."
  • Businesses across the Cleveland Fed district told Hammack that pricing pressures are broadening rather than fading, while consumers are "expressing despair over persistently higher prices."
  • "A higher federal funds rate would help restrain economic activity and reduce inflationary pressures," Hammack said.

What to watch: The officials are not calling for an aggressive tightening campaign. Instead, they said small moves now while the labor market remains healthy would reduce the risk of larger moves later.

  • "[A] potential series of small policy moves would be better than waiting and eventually concluding that even bolder actions were necessary," Kashkari wrote.
  • "Modest action in the near term would reduce the likelihood of needing to take sharper action later," Logan wrote.

The bottom line: The coming months will determine whether these arguments become the consensus inside the Warsh Fed.

item.title: The issue CEOs can't afford to ignore
item.description:
Data: Brunswick Group and Echelon Insights; Chart: Sara Wise/Axios

CEOs face an increasingly skeptical American public that's laser-focused on affordability and fairness, according to polling from the Brunswick Group and Echelon Insights provided first to Axios.

Why it matters: With the midterms less than 100 days away, the results show corporate leaders need to build trust through consistency and neutrality — rather than trying to chase political headwinds.

By the numbers: 41% of Americans surveyed said a topic linked to affordability (cost of living, the economy, jobs) is the biggest issue facing the country right now.

  • Asked what they'd tell CEOs about life in America today, a quarter of respondents pointed to high costs, while another 23% cited greed or inequality.

Between the lines: This is all happening as upcoming AI IPOs could mint some of the richest people in human history, even as those same executives have walked back their predictions of mass job loss from the technology.

  • Even still, 87% of Americans think our economic system works well for large companies — but only about half think it does the same for people like them.

The bottom line: Even in our age of insane political volatility, it's still the economy, stupid.

  • The full results.

item.title: Trump administration's health leadership reboot sputters
item.description:
The Department of Health and Human Services keeps saying it's turning over a new leaf, but it has only been partially successful — and controversial vaccine policymaking appears to be back on the table.

Why it matters: Though the agency reset was launched with the midterm elections in mind, it's already under strain and the elections are still more than three months away.

State of play: Until this week, the administration had spent most of this year toning down its approach to vaccines, after it became clear through polling that vaccine skepticism was a political liability for the GOP in the midterm elections.

  • But it wasn't just vaccines. The Food and Drug Administration had become dysfunctional enough that critics were warning of irreparable harms to the biotech industry and lost cures for patients, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has been without a Senate-confirmed director for the vast majority of Trump's second term.

At the same time, HHS elevated people with much more traditional backgrounds to senior positions within the department, most notably installing Chris Klomp effectively as chief of staff.

  • Former FDA commissioner Marty Makary and top regulator Vinay Prasad both left their jobs in the following months, signaling what the biopharma industry hoped would be a reset on a relationship that had become poisonous.
  • Other controversial personnel either left the administration or — in the case of surgeon general nominee Casey Means — failed to be confirmed.

Where it stands: The projection of a return to business as usual experienced some serious cracks this week.

  • The Senate confirmation of Sean Kaufman, the administration's nominee to lead the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, seemed to be in trouble over his past anti-vaccine statements, though the Senate health committee did approve his nomination Thursday.

And most prominently, the WSJ reported that President Trump has been pressuring Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to do more on vaccines, including probing the alleged connection between vaccines and autism and reducing the number of shots children receive.

  • "💯 true," a source close to HHS and the White House texted Axios in response to the story.
  • That's a stark departure from White House staff urging the department to tone it down — but a testament to the president's genuine commitment to the topic.
  • Scientists have repeatedly said there's no evidence of a connection between vaccines and autism.

The other side: The administration's nominee to lead the CDC, Erica Schwartz, was approved by the Senate health committee with significantly less drama Thursday, even earning a Democrat's vote.

  • And while the FDA is lacking permanent leadership, both the acting commissioner and the acting heads of drug regulation have received widespread praise from industry and other critics of the agency under Makary's tenure.
  • Klomp, who has been nominated as deputy secretary, continues to be largely regarded as competent and a steadying hand.
  • HHS said in a statement: "We have an exceptional team in place across the Department, that is dedicated to serving the American people and carrying out President Trump's bold vision to reverse the chronic disease epidemic, restore trust in public health, and put prevention at the center of health policy as we Make America Healthy Again."

Between the lines: The likelihood that controversial vaccine policy returns with a vengeance post-midterms is completely underappreciated across Washington.

  • Sources close to the administration are confident that vaccine-skeptical rhetoric and policy actions will resume in a few months.
  • "I have full expectation that many of MAHA's goals will reappear after midterms. They'll actually get finalized in the second half of the administration, and the real question is what happens in the next administration?" said David Mansdoerfer, a senior HHS official during Trump's first term.

What they're saying: Parents' "questions and concerns about America's skyrocketing autism rates have long been ignored if not mocked. That changed the day President Trump took office, and the Trump administration is committed to leaving no stone unturned to finally address these concerns with Gold Standard Science," White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement.

The intrigue: Trump's urgency could add longevity to Kennedy's tenure. There's been rampant speculation about whether the secretary will leave the administration after the midterm elections, with many sources believing he'll be gone after they're over.

  • "Of course this means that the Secretary will stay to the end of the Administration," the source close to HHS and the White House told me.
  • "He's been stymied time and again by staff who were worried about the political optics of questioning vaccines. Now he can tell them the President ordered him to do more, and when they try to block him on whatever is next he can march into the Oval."

Reality check: A lot of what Kennedy's critics feared HHS would do on vaccines under his leadership either never happened or was blocked by the courts.

  • But that doesn't preclude those things from happening in the future, particularly during the second half of the Trump administration.

"I knew all along that Trump had these feelings on vaccines. I don't think I fully appreciated how much he was pushing," said Richard Hughes, the attorney leading the legal fight against the HHS vaccine schedule changes.

  • "It's concerning that the president may continue to try to break the law and interfere with what should be evidence-based vaccine policy based on his deeply held, deeply flawed views of science," he added.

Yes, but: Efforts to push vaccine policy or rhetoric won't receive carte-blanche approval within the administration, even without the political considerations of the midterms.

  • "There is a strong desire to ensure any research is done to the highest standards, is validated, etc.," one senior administration official said.

The bottom line: "Administrations typically get more brazen in the second half of the second term when it comes to policy ideas," Mansdoerfer said.

  • "I think you have a president who has a firm belief in many of these same lines of thinking as Secretary Kennedy does, who will say, 'This is my legacy, I am going to do this because I think it is the right thing.'"

item.title: Exclusive: FBI gets voter's IP address in new fraud probe tactic
item.description:
The Trump administration has a new tactic for trying to isolate cases of alleged voter fraud — digging into the IP addresses of those who went online to register to vote.

  • The FBI recently obtained the IP address of someone who registered online in South Carolina, according to documents first shared with Axios.

Why it matters: The bureau's request for the address, which state and local officials complied with, offers a glimpse of how federal authorities are stepping up their probe of voter rolls and registration practices under pressure from President Trump.

  • The president's persistent complaints about the 2020 election have expanded into federal investigations that also involve the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security.

It's unclear how often the FBI plans to take the extraordinary step of seeking IP addresses, but its push in South Carolina has broad implications nationwide: 43 states allow some form of online voter registration.

  • An IP address would show a user's geographic location and service provider, but not their specific identity. It could tell whether the user was outside a state or even the U.S., for example.
  • Trump has claimed that operatives in China and elsewhere have tried to influence U.S. elections.

The big picture: As the bureau investigates South Carolina, ICE has been requesting voter data in Texas and North Carolina.

  • The Justice Department, meanwhile, is trying to get voter rolls from states that have resisted sharing registration information, and is suing 30 states and Washington, D.C., for that access.

Critics say it's a federal intrusion rooted in Trump's baseless claims about widespread fraud in the 2020 election.

  • "The administration has gone down every rabbit hole, pursued every possible avenue to undermine the confidence in the integrity of the federal election process and to undermine the process itself," said Robert Weiner, former senior counsel at DOJ's civil rights division and director of the Voting Rights Project at the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights.

Driving the news: An FBI agent in South Carolina stepped up the probe there in March by asking state and local officials for the IP address of a voter's online registration, according to emails revealed in a public records request by Democracy Forward, which shared them with Axios.

  • The email exchange between the FBI and the general counsel of South Carolina's State Election Commission is partially redacted. The general counsel didn't respond to a request for comment.
  • Another exchange, under the subject line, "Voter Investigation" shows the FBI agent receiving the voter's digital information in June.
  • The FBI didn't respond to several requests for comment.

What they're saying: "It is not common" to get this kind of request, York County (S.C.) election official Alan Helms told Axios. "In my tenure as an election official, going on 20 years, that is the first interaction with law enforcement."

  • Helms said his office complied with the request, as is permitted under the law.
  • "It's not typical for the FBI to be calling state election officials and just asking and conducting a fishing expedition to see private voter data," a former senior Justice Department official told Axios. "It's not typical and it's not appropriate."

Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dillon has sent a letter warning election officials about statutes that ban non-citizens from voting in federal elections. DHS general counsel James Percival issued a memo asking immigration officials to use any voting-related crimes as evidence in deportation proceedings for noncitizens.

  • Dillon's office also announced it would send poll watchers to three Arizona counties ahead of that state's primary on July 21.

Zoom in: Since the Trump administration claimed to have found hundreds of thousands of voters registered illegally or deceased across the U.S., New Jersey has revealed that about 6,600 noncitizens had registered to vote because of a software error.

  • New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherill (D) said her team's investigation so far has removed about 4,500 people from the state's voter rolls, and that some people initially identified as ineligible actually might be eligible to vote.
  • Trump's administration is holding up New Jersey, a Democrat-led state, as an example of a state with election issues and is trying to force it to share its full voter rolls with federal investigators. So far, it's resisting.

Flashback: A similar software issue was investigated in North Carolina in 2021. The state found about 700 potential noncitizens had registered and more than 100 of them had voted in 2016.

  • No charges brought in most cases because the registration error was no one's fault. In some cases, voters were registered despite acknowledging on a DMV form that they weren't citizens. Others were registered after leaving the question blank.

item.title: How extreme weather is shaping tomorrow's electric grid
item.description:
A series of dangerous heat waves this summer — including one that has left 17 states under an emergency federal order — are putting the electric grid under an intense real-world stress test.

Why it matters: Successive summer heat waves are forcing utilities to rethink how they prepare the grid for longer and more frequent periods of extreme stress.

  • They're raising questions about whether the electric grid can keep pace with surging demand from both climate change and the AI-driven electricity boom.

State of play: Heat waves create a double challenge by increasing electricity demand for air-conditioning while reducing the efficiency of some power plants.

Zoom in: Texas has become one of the nation's biggest proving grounds for grid modernization since the deadly 2021 winter storm exposed major weaknesses.

  • The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which operates most of the state's grid, has since handled record seasonal demand with the help of rapid battery expansion, mandatory weatherization, improved forecasting and expanded demand response.
  • This month, the Public Utility Commission of Texas approved standards requiring large data centers to disconnect in a controlled way during grid disturbances to help protect grid stability.

Yes, but: ERCOT told state lawmakers that statewide electric demand will reach about 175,000 megawatts by 2032 — almost double the record number that was set this month.

Between the lines: "Texas has been enormously proactive" in building transmission and adding solar, wind and batteries, retired UC Berkeley electrical engineering professor Sascha von Meier tells Axios.

  • But rapid growth in electricity demand from AI data centers is creating a new challenge, she says.
  • Aidan Tuohy of the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit energy research and development organization, says utilities are shifting from planning for a single peak hour to ensuring they have enough resources to remain reliable throughout prolonged periods of extreme heat.
  • "There isn't one specific resource that's coming up and saving the day or anything like that," says Tuohy, EPRI's director of research and development. "It's a mix, and that diversity is actually a big part of the equation."

Zoom out: A growing number of U.S. utilities are linking home batteries, solar panels and EV chargers through software to virtual power plants that can supply electricity or reduce demand during periods of grid stress.

  • "In California, we've had very positive experiences with battery storage and the way that it has performed during extreme peak demand days," von Meier says.
  • She points to a California Independent System Operator study that called batteries "invaluable for reliability" after helping the state avoid rotating outages during a record 2022 heat wave.

Tuohy says utilities are increasingly looking at whether large data centers can become flexible grid resources rather than simply new sources of demand.

  • Early results from an EPRI demonstration in Arizona showed a participating AI data center reduced electricity use by 25% over three hours during a simulated peak-demand event.

What we're watching: Von Meier expects that five years from now, electric grids will become more agile and flexible, out of necessity.

  • "We may find it no longer realistic to accommodate unlimited demand at uniform reliability across entire interconnections at a reasonable price," she says.
  • "Instead, we will value efficiency, flexible backup options, including storage, self-generation and microgrids, and more active management of electric demand. All the key technologies exist today."

The bottom line: Reliability "is going to be won or lost," Tuohy says. "It's not the individual components. It's how they all work together."

Go deeper: The power decisions that could shape the next century

item.title: Publishers are losing Google traffic as AI answers replace links
item.description:
The way your work shows up in a digital-dominated world is changing lightning fast, starting with the total collapse of Google Search traffic.

Why it matters: Google has basically stopped sending people to websites (including our site) for answers and information. Instead, it's using AI to answer them on its platform, in its words.

  • Chartbeat data shared with Axios shows Google Search traffic to publishers fell 34% over the past year.
  • That pain is regressive. Over the past two years, small publishers lost 60% of referrals from search overall, medium publishers 47%, large publishers 22%.
  • This is a gut punch to all of us who operate online because people who search arrive with specific needs and intent, so they tend to be more valuable than a random passer-by from X or Facebook.

At the same time, LinkedIn, Reddit and other massive platforms are getting jammed with AI-created content, making it harder to stand out — or decipher real from fake.

  • To that end, Substack announced a partnership last week with AI-detection software Pangram, specifically calling out LinkedIn while arguing that "platforms that reward fakeness will create a race to the bottom."

Between the lines: Any smart person who primarily does business online is already anticipating the shift to an LLM, ChatGPT-like world.

  • It starts with GEO — the term for shaping how content shows up inside LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT. This is the modern version of SEO. It's early, and it's a black box. But there's no time to waste.

The future: My theory is all of us will need to rethink and reformat our content to meet human AND AI needs.

  • Turns out, our Smart Brevity format — most important point first, context second, information stacked in order of importance, often in bullet form — works wonders with AI.
  • We're among the top publishers surfaced by the leading LLMs, so we're working with companies to see if they can achieve similar results.

It's crucial to get ahead of this problem. At Axios, we're already figuring out how we can:

  • Show up inside LLMs now.
  • Improve that standing.
  • Offset reliance on search and open web.
  • Connect with audiences in a post-open-web world. (Direct relationships via things like newsletters and events are a good start.)

What's next: The agent wave is coming. Smart publishers have largely stopped treating AI engines as a referral source and now treat them as a distribution layer.

  • Soon, the "customer" reading a website, comparing prices and learning about a product will often be someone's AI agent as the middleman.

📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

item.title: Inside Europe's lessons on AI safety as U.S. rules loom
item.description:
Europe and the United Kingdom are fine-tuning their approach to AI model testing as a deadline looms for the U.S. government to set rules of the road.

Why it matters: U.S. allies for years have been grappling with the same AI safety questions the Trump administration now faces.

  • Wherever the U.S. lands in its AI framework, architects of the EU and U.K. approaches say it would be just the start.

The big picture: President Trump began his second term by scrapping his predecessor's AI strategy and pursuing an anti-regulatory regime.

  • But as AI models rapidly grew more powerful, the Trump administration has found itself developing an oversight framework and deciding exactly what should be covered.
  • Under Trump's executive order, the administration is due to release its voluntary AI framework by Aug. 1.
  • The Trump administration is weighing a unified pitch from OpenAI and Anthropic to create "an equal playing field" where highly capable models are all covered, regardless of whether they're open- or closed-source, according to one source familiar with the discussions.

The EU, meanwhile, has treated AI safety as a sustained technical and policy project for several years.

  • It's a fluid approach to cybersecurity use cases where previous events inform future rules.

Zoom in: One lesson from Europe is to start with specific threat scenarios.

  • Researchers begin with historical data on threats such as biological weapons, then measure how much AI increases a bad actor's capabilities and whether that creates a systemic risk to society, CEO and co-founder of AI evaluation firm EquiStamp Chris Canal told Axios.
  • Other key lessons from the EU process include tying benchmarking — testing AI models against standardized evaluations to measure their capabilities and risks — to specific scenarios, such as bioweapons or government database hacks.
  • The EU also emphasizes multiple, independent verifications rather than relying solely on companies' own assessments.
  • Canal worked with the EU and U.K. governments to shape their approaches to AI regulation.

Zoom out: The EU commits to getting buy-in from the scientific community, grounding AI risk thresholds in peer-reviewed science before embedding them into policy and pushing researchers to publish their methodologies.

  • By comparison, the U.S. relies mainly on internal or industry-driven standards.
  • Technical experts are also flocking to the private sector, particularly in the U.S. and U.K.

What they're saying: "There have been several times where we're working with someone on the [U.K.] government side, and they suddenly put in their two weeks' notice, maybe less, and then they have a great position at OpenAI," Canal said.

The bottom line: Governments are starting to coalesce around cyber risks, but the U.S. and its allies are only beginning to map AI's broader challenges.

item.title: Divided Democrats face a moment of truth in Michigan Senate primary
item.description:
Democratic socialists look like they're about to rack up a stunning new victory: Their candidate in Michigan's Senate Democratic primary has the momentum heading into Tuesday's primary.

Why it matters: A win by Abdul El-Sayed in the swing state would turbocharge the party's left flank and validate establishment fears about the party's direction.

The big picture: Establishment Democrats have watched in horror as democratic socialist candidates pull off one win after another in House primaries this year. The Michigan primary brings the ideological clash to its biggest stage yet.

  • El-Sayed, who's backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is taking on an establishment favorite in a race that's become a proxy fight between the party's far-left and center-left wings.
  • Democratic leaders have gone all-in for Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens because they think she can win moderate voters — and El-Sayed can't.
  • But El-Sayed has vaulted to a hefty lead in the final stretch of the campaign. One survey this week had him up 15 points. Other polls have shown him with smaller but still substantial leads.
  • The political stakes don't get much higher. If Democrats lose Michigan on Nov. 3, they almost certainly aren't winning the Senate.

State of play: Together with Zohran Mamdani's victory in the New York City mayor's race, democratic socialists have proven they're not on the periphery of the party anymore — the center of gravity has shifted unmistakably in their direction.

  • A CNN poll out Thursday showed about a third of Democratic voters identify as democratic socialists — and they're the most motivated to turn out.
  • But winning House primaries is one thing. Winning a statewide Senate primary in one of the nation's premier battlegrounds is another.

Driving the news: El-Sayed has gained ground as the campaign progressed.

  • Stevens had a sizable lead early on, with El-Sayed in second and state senator Mallory McMorrow trailing. But El-Sayed moved up over the past two months, and in the weeks since McMorrow dropped out in early July, established himself as the frontrunner in polls.
  • Stevens is the consensus choice of the Democratic establishment. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer lined up behind her early. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer came aboard late, with an endorsement last week.
  • The primary is also a monumental moment for AIPAC. The pro-Israel organization and affiliated groups have poured roughly $30 million into boosting Stevens — the most it's ever spent in a single race, per the AP.
  • Israel is a central dividing line in the race: Stevens has described herself as a "proud pro-Israel Democrat." El-Sayed has accused the country of committing genocide in Gaza.

The intrigue: The bigger question for Democrats is whether the party is undergoing the kind of makeover Republicans experienced a decade ago with Donald Trump — or if the democratic socialist surge is confined to the bluest enclaves.

  • No primary this year will offer a clearer answer than Michigan's.
  • Democratic socialists argue they're filling a vacuum. Even as establishment Democrats say El-Sayed can't win, they've struggled to articulate their own vision beyond "Trump is bad" and "stuff is too expensive."

The other side: Republicans dejected by President Trump's record low approval rating and unpopular war are suddenly reveling in the opposition's leftward lunge.

  • Trump has adopted a campaign strategy that boils down to: "You may not like me, but do you really want those crazy communists instead?"
  • El-Sayed doesn't identify as a democratic socialist, but DSA organizers are going all out to help him. Sanders (I-Vt.) and Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) have both campaigned for him.
  • Trump undoubtedly would cast the epidemiologist and former Rhodes scholar as another Democratic "communist."

What we're watching: An El-Sayed win would only be step one for the democratic socialist cause. To truly show the far-left wing can compete in the most competitive terrain, he'd need to win in November against Rep. Mike Rogers, the presumptive Republican nominee.

What we're watching: An El-Sayed win would only be step one for the democratic socialist cause. To truly show the far-left wing can compete in the most competitive terrain, he'd need to win in November against Rep. Mike Rogers, the presumptive Republican nominee.

item.title: Trump touts "historic" agreement to disarm Hamas, rebuild Gaza
item.description:
President Trump announced Thursday that his Board of Peace had reached an agreement with Hamas to disarm and transfer civilian and security control of Gaza to a new Palestinian technocratic government.

Why it matters: If implemented, the agreement would represent a dramatic breakthrough in Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan and clear the way for reconstruction of the devastated enclave.

  • But the deal requires Hamas and Israel to complete a complicated series of reciprocal and independently verified steps over roughly seven to eight months.
  • Israeli officials remain deeply skeptical that Hamas will surrender its weapons, while comments from a senior Hamas official suggest the sequencing of disarmament and Israel's withdrawal could still be contested.

What they're saying: "Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," Trump wrote Thursday evening on Truth Social.

  • "This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY," he added.

State of play: Two U.S. officials said Hamas had agreed to the terms of the deal after months of what one senior administration official described as "very delicate" negotiations with mediators Qatar, Turkey and Egypt.

  • Implementation is expected to begin in the coming weeks, the senior U.S. official said.
  • A Board of Peace official said this is the first time Hamas and the other Palestinian factions in Gaza have agreed to demilitarize the enclave and transfer responsibility for security and civilian services to a technocratic government.

Under the agreement, Hamas would relinquish any role in governing Gaza. The new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) would serve as an alternative to Hamas and the Palestinian Authority.

  • "It will work for the people of Gaza," the senior U.S. official said.

Reality check: Hamas official Ghazi Hamad confirmed to Al Jazeera that "difficult" negotiations had produced an agreement, but his description raised immediate questions about its implementation.

  • "We will not take any steps regarding disarmament before Israel withdraws from the Gaza Strip," Hamad said. He added that the NCAG would carry out disarmament without Israeli involvement.
  • That appears to differ from Trump's description of a "carefully structured" and phased process in which Israeli forces withdraw as disarmament is completed.
  • U.S. and Board of Peace officials said implementation would proceed through reciprocal, independently verified steps, while acknowledging that the timetable for Israel's withdrawal is still being finalized.

The big picture: Large parts of Gaza were destroyed during the war, and most of its 2 million residents continue to live in tents or makeshift shelters.

  • Food and other aid are entering Gaza in large quantities, but the humanitarian situation remains dire.
  • The Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry says nearly 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the Oct. 10, 2025, ceasefire. Some were Hamas militants, while many others were civilians, including children.

Zoom in: The agreement is based on the principle that Gaza will have one government, one legal system and one legitimate security authority. The demilitarization process is expected to take between 200 and 250 days and to proceed through one part of Gaza at a time.

  • Hamas' civilian police would first transfer their weapons to a new Palestinian police force under the technocratic government.
  • Hamas' heavy weapons would then be decommissioned and placed in secure storage, while its tunnels and weapons factories would be dismantled.
  • Small arms would be collected in accordance with Palestinian law.
  • All other militias in Gaza, including anti-Hamas factions armed by Israel during the war, would also be required to surrender their weapons.

The NCAG would assume authority over each area only after a monitoring mechanism verified that the relevant commitments had been fulfilled.

  • At the end of the process, the technocratic government and its police force would have a monopoly on weapons in Gaza, the Board of Peace official said.

How it works: Under the agreement, an international stabilization force would help train the new Palestinian police, assist with weapons collection, and deploy between Palestinian-controlled areas and Israeli forces.

  • A Board of Peace official said the agreement was designed around "zero trust" because Hamas and Israel each made clear from the outset that they did not trust the other side.
  • The process would not advance from one stage to the next until monitors verified that both sides had met their obligations.
  • The goal is to avoid a situation in which the technocratic government controls Gaza during the day while armed factions retain power at night, the official said.

The other side: Israel's withdrawal would proceed gradually under a timetable that is still being finalized.

  • Trump said Israeli forces would withdraw as disarmament was completed and the international force and new Palestinian police assumed responsibility for security.
  • Israel would also halt military operations and targeted killings in Gaza, except in cases involving an imminent threat.
  • "All military activity in Gaza will have to cease — both from Israel and Hamas," the Board of Peace official said.

Inside the room: The senior U.S. official said the Trump administration coordinated closely with Israel throughout the negotiations.

  • The administration also intends to ensure Israel fulfills its commitments under the agreement, despite Israel's skepticism that Hamas will disarm.
  • "We are not asking Israel for anything other than to implement their commitments under the 20-point plan," the official said.
  • "If they do not do that, President Trump will be very disappointed. I do not think the Israelis would want to escalate things with us right now."

Behind the scenes: Egypt, Qatar and Turkey exerted intense pressure on Hamas to accept the agreement, according to two sources familiar with the negotiations.

  • A key figure was Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, who hosted the talks and has a close relationship with Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya, U.S. officials and others familiar with the negotiations said.

The intrigue: During a recent visit to Iran for the funeral of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, a Hamas delegation met with senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officials, according to a source with knowledge of the meeting.

  • The IRGC officials urged Hamas not to rush into signing the agreement and to play for time, the source said.
  • A senior U.S. official also claimed Iran tried to convince Hamas not to sign the deal, but said the group chose not to listen.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Inside Trump's Senate playbook
item.description:
President Trump has three go-to moves for GOP senators who frustrate him: persuade them when he can, ignore them when he must and bully them at will.

Why it matters: The approach doesn't always produce results. But it almost always provides drama.

Persuade: Trump dispatched two top deputies to the Senate GOP lunch on Wednesday to make the case, in person, for a third reconciliation bill with elements of the SAVE Act.

  • Then he sent in the big guns. Chief of Staff Susie Wiles huddled with the Senate GOP leaders shortly after their lunch.
  • When Trump faced a Senate rebuke over the Iran conflict last month, the White House aggressively lobbied wavering Republicans to flip their votes.

Ignore: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche doesn't need Senate confirmation to do the job, Trump declared on Truth Social on Thursday.

  • He can serve as acting attorney general indefinitely. Problem solved.

Bully: Trump began the week by demanding that Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) scrap the filibuster and pass the SAVE Act.

  • "Remember, stupidity always brings LOSING & DEATH!" Trump wrote.

What we're watching: Bullying appeared to be Trump's preferred tactic this week. By Wednesday, he was openly questioning whether Thune should remain majority leader.

  • Thune's best defense was to downplay his own powers.
  • "He thinks I can wave the magic wand," Thune told Politico. "I wish it were that easy."
  • Trump's penchant for bullying has emboldened some senators to stand their ground — such as John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who have blocked Blanche's nomination. Both will be out of the Senate in January.

Zoom in: Trump's anger with the Senate keeps flaring, despite Thune's success in rapidly confirming his nominees.

  • With Jay Clayton's confirmation as director of national intelligence, the GOP-led Senate has confirmed 515 of Trump's nominees — with another batch of 74 on the way.
  • That's a faster pace than the first administration and leaves only a handful of civilian nominations remaining on the Executive Calendar.
  • Trump now has the authority to install many of the remaining nominees in acting roles across the federal government.

Zoom out: With one week left before the August recess, Senate Republican vibes are going from bad to worse.

  • New polls show Americans continuing to sour on the GOP.
  • The MAGA base is still enraged over the SAVE Act.
  • Everything from the NDAA to crypto legislation is hitting roadblocks.

And Trump doesn't appear interested in easing the pressure on his own party.

The bottom line: Trump reserves the right to toggle among his three approaches, depending on his needs and mood.

  • And while he can ignore the Senate on some personnel, he can't ignore it on legislation. He still needs 50 votes — or, in some cases, 60.
  • "When crazy becomes the norm, it feels pretty routine," one GOP senator told Axios.

item.title: Anthropic says three Claude models reached real-world systems during cyber tests
item.description:
Some of Anthropic's most powerful models — including Mythos 5 and an internal research model — gained unauthorized access to real-world systems during pre-deployment cybersecurity testing, the company said Thursday.

Why it matters: OpenAI's and Anthropic's latest disclosures show frontier AI models reaching real-world systems during safety testing, raising new questions about how labs secure their evaluation environments.

The big picture: Anthropic said a misunderstanding between the company and one of its testing partners left the evaluation environment connected to the internet.

  • Anthropic reviewed more than 141,000 cybersecurity evaluation runs after OpenAI disclosed that several of its models accessed Hugging Face infrastructure during testing.

Driving the news: Anthropic said in a blog post that three of its models compromised real-world systems belonging to three organizations.

  • The incidents — which involved Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and an internal research model not intended for general release — happened during evaluations run with third-party testing partner Irregular, Anthropic said.
  • In each case, the models were asked to complete a "capture-the-flag" exercise: a basic cybersecurity test where players try to find pieces of information intentionally left on a different machine or network.

Context: The earliest incidents happened in April, Anthropic said. The company reached out to all three organizations. Per Anthropic, two organizations it was able to reach had not previously detected the activity.

  • Anthropic did not name the three organizations whose assets were accessed.
  • An Irregular spokesperson told Axios that while its own investigation is ongoing, the company appreciates "Anthropic's collaboration and transparency" and they "look forward to continuing to work together to advance security.

Yes, but: Unlike OpenAI's incident, Anthropic said its models did not exploit a zero-day vulnerability to gain internet access. Instead, internet access was available because of the testing environment's configuration.

  • Anthropic says that in its evaluation prompt to Claude, it said the model would be operating in a simulated environment with no internet access.
  • But due to the misunderstanding with the evaluation partner, the evaluation environments were connected to the internet, causing the models to treat real-world systems as if they were part of the exercise.

Reality check: Similar to the OpenAI case, Anthropic was evaluating its models without the additional safeguards the company deploys on publicly available models, allowing researchers to measure the underlying models' capabilities.

  • Those guardrails would have blocked these behaviors, Anthropic said in its report.

Zoom in: In each of the cases, Claude used basic hacking techniques — including exploiting weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints — to access the real-world systems.

Zoom out: In the first incident, the fictional company that Opus 4.7 was asked to target shared a name with an active, real-world website. After failing to reach the fictional target, Claude used its internet access to find the website that shared the name of the fictional company. Claude then compromised the website.

  • In the second case, Mythos 5 built and uploaded a malicious Python package to PyPI, the public repository where Python software is published, believing it was part of a simulation.
  • The package remained online for about an hour, during which it was downloaded and run on 15 real systems. One of those systems belonged to a security company that automatically installs Python packages to scan them for malware, allowing Claude's code to exfiltrate credentials and access additional infrastructure.
  • In the third case, when Anthropic's internal research test model couldn't reach its intended fictional target in testing, the model scanned roughly 9,000 targets and eventually found and compromised one company's internet-facing application.
  • However, during part of its testing run, this model realized that it had ended up in a cloud account "with no connection to the capture-the-flag challenge" and ceased its attack.

Between the lines: Both OpenAI's and Anthropic's incidents suggest the models remained focused on completing their assigned evaluations rather than pursuing independent goals.

  • Earlier this week, Axios reported that the OpenAI agent that accessed a third-party system during the Hugging Face breach did so because it hosted information related to CyberGym, the project behind the benchmark it was trying to solve.

What's next: Anthropic and Irregular are continuing their own investigations into how the incidents occurred. Anthropic also said it has halted cyber evaluations that could access the internet while it reviews its testing infrastructure.

Go deeper: The people testing AI for danger can't keep up

Editor's note: This story was corrected to reflect that a misunderstanding between Anthropic and one of its testing partners left the models' evaluation environment connected to the internet. (The models did not, per Anthropic, "escape" their testing environment.)

item.title: Tim Cook says Apple may charge for AI Siri
item.description:
Apple hinted Thursday that heavy users of its revamped Siri may have to pay for access.

Why it matters: It's the first time that Apple has confirmed it will charge for the new AI-powered voice assistant.

What they're saying: In a conference call to discuss Apple's most recent quarterly earnings, CEO Tim Cook said Apple is still developing its plan to address the higher computing costs that will come with the improved voice assistant.

  • "We do believe there will be people that want to use it a lot, and so we will have some kind of upgrade possibilities on iCloud+," Cook said during a call to discuss Apple's most recent quarterly earnings.
  • Apple has also said that users will need a paid iCloud subscription to take advantage of a new home security feature built into the next version of IOS.

The big picture: Apple unveiled its long-delayed Siri upgrade at its developer conference in June. A public beta began this month, with broad availability due in the fall alongside new iPhones.

  • Cook says the positive early reviews of the new Siri "underscores our philosophy that building AI that is private and based on personal context can change how users find information and get things done with our products in a way that truly enriches their lives."

Zoom in: Bloomberg and others have predicted that usage of some features of the new iPhone operating system might require a paid iCloud subscription.

Between the lines: Apple is relying in part on Google Gemini models to help power the new Siri.

item.title: Inside the $2 million effort to oust Rep. Andy Ogles in his Republican primary
item.description:
A super PAC that has invested millions to unseat Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) is putting another $700,000 behind his GOP primary challenger in the final week of the campaign, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Ogles was already facing one his most perilous reelection battle to date, with Democrats making him one of their top targets in November. But first he has to get the nomination, which is not a done deal.

  • Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, the clean-energy aligned super PAC working to primary Ogles, commissioned a poll that has him leading his challenger, Charlie Hatcher, by just four percentage points.
  • The survey, first shared with Axios, had Ogles at 37% and Hatcher at 33% among 400 likely Republican primary voters interviewed between July 26 and 28.
  • It was conducted by Tusk Strategies and has a margin of error of plus-or-minus 5 percentage points.

Driving the news: ITC is "committing an additional $700,000 in paid media for the final week of the race" on top of the $1.3 million it had already spent as of Wednesday, according to a press release first shared with Axios.

  • Renewable energy executives are using the super PAC to punish Republican lawmakers for anti-wind and solar policies, such as the rollback of clean energy tax credits in the One Big, Beautiful Bill.
  • "Our campaign is here to show that politicians who oppose clean energy do so at their own political peril. Andy Ogles is next," the group's chair, Tom Matzzie, who is also CEO of solar company CleanChoice Energy, said in a statement.
  • The group spent heavily to defeat Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) in the GOP primary runoff for Texas attorney general. Roy lost to Mayes Middleton.

The other side: "As the Trump-endorsed candidate in this race, I am being targeted by left-wing liberals from California because I am one of President Trump's closest allies," Ogles said in a statement to Axios.

  • "They want to stop Trump-endorsed MAGA warriors from delivering for the American people. This desperate attempt to SILENCE me is futile. I will not be silent and I will never stop fighting to put America First."
  • Ogles noted that ITC's top donor is cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen, who is also a major donor to California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D).
  • In addition to its spending against Roy and Ogles, the group spent $125,000 to support Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa), who voted for the OBBB but fought to preserve the IRA tax credits.

State of play: Despite Ogles' incumbency and crucial support from Trump, Hatcher has some things going for him.

  • A former Tennessee Commissioner of Agriculture, Hatcher is backed by some party heavyweights, including former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam and former Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue.
  • Ogles is also running in drastically new territory after Tennessee's mid-cycle redistricting, which saw his district take in more rural, agricultural areas that Hatcher's camp believes will favor them.
  • Hatcher campaign consultant John Newman told Axios his candidate "relates to folks in the newly drawn congressional district much better than the current occupant."

By the numbers: ITC has also swamped Ogles' biggest backer, the House Freedom Fund, which has spent just under $500,000 on the race.

  • Hatcher has also out-raised the incumbent, bringing in $720,000 in contributions as of July 17 and coming into the final stretch with $105,000 in cash-on-hand.
  • Ogles raised $610,000 and had just $58,000 in cash by the same point, but his campaign owed about $70,000 in debt.

Between the lines: Ogles has also been the subject of significant public controversy in recent years.

  • He is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for his campaign finances and previously faced an Justice Department probe that was shut down after Trump returned to office last year.
  • He has also repeatedly drawn condemnation from colleagues for making Islamophobic public statements, such as writing on social media in March that "Muslims don't belong in American society."

Yes, but: Ogles still has incumbency and Trump, which are highly significant factors in most Republican primaries.

  • The president held a tele-rally on Ogles' behalf Tuesday, urging listeners to "get out and vote for Andy Ogles," who he said has "been a friend of mine."
  • Tennessee Republicans say Ogles is in real danger but probably still the favorite, with one U.S. House member from the state telling Axios, "If he works, he wins."
  • But, this lawmaker warned, Ogles "still could lose [the] general" in November.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional comment from Ogles.
item.content:encoded:
A super PAC that has invested millions to unseat Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) is putting another $700,000 behind his GOP primary challenger in the final week of the campaign, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Ogles was already facing one his most perilous reelection battle to date, with Democrats making him one of their top targets in November. But first he has to get the nomination, which is not a done deal.

  • Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, the clean-energy aligned super PAC working to primary Ogles, commissioned a poll that has him leading his challenger, Charlie Hatcher, by just four percentage points.
  • The survey, first shared with Axios, had Ogles at 37% and Hatcher at 33% among 400 likely Republican primary voters interviewed between July 26 and 28.
  • It was conducted by Tusk Strategies and has a margin of error of plus-or-minus 5 percentage points.

Driving the news: ITC is "committing an additional $700,000 in paid media for the final week of the race" on top of the $1.3 million it had already spent as of Wednesday, according to a press release first shared with Axios.

  • Renewable energy executives are using the super PAC to punish Republican lawmakers for anti-wind and solar policies, such as the rollback of clean energy tax credits in the One Big, Beautiful Bill.
  • "Our campaign is here to show that politicians who oppose clean energy do so at their own political peril. Andy Ogles is next," the group's chair, Tom Matzzie, who is also CEO of solar company CleanChoice Energy, said in a statement.
  • The group spent heavily to defeat Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) in the GOP primary runoff for Texas attorney general. Roy lost to Mayes Middleton.

The other side: "As the Trump-endorsed candidate in this race, I am being targeted by left-wing liberals from California because I am one of President Trump's closest allies," Ogles said in a statement to Axios.

  • "They want to stop Trump-endorsed MAGA warriors from delivering for the American people. This desperate attempt to SILENCE me is futile. I will not be silent and I will never stop fighting to put America First."
  • Ogles noted that ITC's top donor is cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen, who is also a major donor to California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D).
  • In addition to its spending against Roy and Ogles, the group spent $125,000 to support Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa), who voted for the OBBB but fought to preserve the IRA tax credits.

State of play: Despite Ogles' incumbency and crucial support from Trump, Hatcher has some things going for him.

  • A former Tennessee Commissioner of Agriculture, Hatcher is backed by some party heavyweights, including former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam and former Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue.

  • He is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for his campaign finances and previously faced an Justice Department probe that was shut down after Trump returned to office last year.

Yes, but: Ogles still has incumbency and Trump, which are highly significant factors in most Republican primaries.

  • The president held a tele-rally on Ogles' behalf Tuesday, urging listeners to "get out and vote for Andy Ogles," who he said has "been a friend of mine."
  • Tennessee Republicans say Ogles is in real danger but probably still the favorite, with one U.S. House member from the state telling Axios, "If he works, he wins."
  • But, this lawmaker warned, Ogles "still could lose [the] general" in November.

item.title: Bessent sets stage for Xi visit in high-level China talk
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a high-level video call with China's vice premier to prepare for the September visit of its president, Xi Jinping, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The call sets the stage for President Trump and Xi to sign future trade deals between the U.S. and China. But there are tensions.

Zoom in: The cordial video conference call between Bessent, Greer and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng lasted more than an hour.

  • "I emphasized that we expect Beijing to fully meet its commitments on rare earths and U.S. agricultural products," Bessent told Axios in a written statement.
  • "We also discussed implementation of the Trade and Investment Boards as a mechanism to secure concrete progress toward a more balanced, fair, and constructive U.S.-China economic relationship."

Between the lines: One source familiar with the talks said that "over the past several months, China adopted or relied upon measures that create new risks for U.S. firms, restrict lawful commercial activity, and seek to deter lawful U.S. national security actions."

  • "This is problematic," the source said. "The U.S. has raised these concerns repeatedly within their trade and economic channel and provided China time to reverse course, but China has continued to escalate and cause chaos.
  • "China's continued escalations will have consequences."

Zoom out: Relations between the two countries have been tense amid the battle for AI supremacy.

  • Trump has sought to limit China from obtaining advanced computer microchips, and Xi threatened to withhold critical minerals needed for advanced computer and weapons technology.
  • At a meeting in Beijing, Trump and Xi appeared to put differences behind them but signed no new deals.
  • But this week, the Trump administration announced plans to ban Chinese robots and power inverters as national security threats.

Adding a new layer of complexity is the Iran war.

  • China is an Iranian ally and, according to Reuters, plans to sell shoulder-fired missiles to Iran. Trump said he would be "disappointed" if the sale went through.
  • Earlier this month, Trump released once-classified documents indicating China meddled in the 2020 election. He then expressed hesitation about pushing the issue with Xi.
  • "They do things and we do things to them. I'll be honest. We do things to them too," Trump told reporters last week. "It's not a one-way street. But we'll be talking to them, yes."

item.title: Trump says he's open to delaying Blanche nomination over GOP defectors
item.description:
President Trump said Thursday that he would have "no objection" to temporarily withdrawing acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination until his Republican opponents are out of office next January.

The big picture: Trump's threat, directed at GOP Sens. Thom Tillis (N.C.) and John Cornyn (Texas), puts Blanche's critics on notice as to what the president deemed "the right thing" after their concerns stalled the acting attorney general's nomination.

  • Cornyn lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger, and current Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Tillis chose not to seek re-election.

Driving the news: "Todd Blanche is a STAR," Trump wrote of his former personal attorney turned Justice Department loyalist.

  • He added that Blanche would "remain, in any event, as Acting."
  • Cornyn had demanded a written guarantee that the administration's controversial $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund" was dead. The fund was born out of a scrutinized settlement agreement between Trump and the IRS.

State of play: A "no" vote from Tillis or Cornyn, who both sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee, would prevent Blanche's nomination from advancing to a confirmation vote before the full Senate.

  • On Wednesday night, the committee postponed a crucial vote on Blanche's nomination over the Republicans' steadfast opposition.

Reality check: Even if the president withdraws Blanche's name for confirmation, he would retain the vast power of the nation's chief law enforcement officer in an acting capacity, as he has since this spring.

What they're saying: "POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis," Cornyn wrote in a post on X.

  • During Blanche's confirmation hearing before a Senate panel earlier this month, Cornyn questioned whether there had been a written agreement to modify the IRS settlement fund, which Blanche said was "just not moving forward."
  • Cornyn does have a point — GOP concerns over the head-turning settlement, which has been lambasted by a federal judge, have already derailed the party's legislative goals.
  • Bashed as a political slush fund that could benefit those convicted in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot, the administration dropped the fund after a federal judge blocked the money's disbursement.

Go deeper: The major controversies stalling Todd Blanche's attorney general nomination

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

item.title: AI-focused hedge fund sells all of its stocks
item.description:
Situational Awareness, an AI-focused hedge fund founded by a former OpenAI researcher, has sold all of its public equities portfolio to Ken Griffin's Citadel, a source tells Axios.

Why it matters: This comes amidst a recent sell-off in AI stocks, particularly chipmakers.

  • News of a sale was first reported by the WSJ.

Catch up quick: Former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner founded Situational Awareness after being fired from OpenAI in 2024, over an alleged information leak that he disputes. It recently reported around $20 billion in assets under management.

  • Early investors included Stripe cofounders Patrick and John Collison, plus former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and ex-Apple employee Daniel Gross.

Zoom in: Just yesterday, the FT reported that Situational Awareness "has sought to raise fresh capital from investors after suffering heavy losses during the recent rout in AI stocks."

  • That seems to have escalated quickly.

item.title: Senate panel approves CDC nominee, controversial HHS pick
item.description:
The Senate health committee approved the nomination of Erica Schwartz for Centers for Disease Control director Thursday, a step toward refilling the depleted ranks of the Trump administration's health care leadership.

  • The committee also approved the nomination of Sean Kaufman, who's in line for assistant secretary for preparedness and response and had been in trouble because of past anti-vaccine statements.

Why it matters: The votes showed Republicans, at least, are still willing to accept the administration's assurances about the nominees even though committee chair Bill Cassidy has made it clear he's uneasy with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s policies.

  • The narrow committee endorsements put both nominees in line for votes to be confirmed by the full Senate, which have yet to be scheduled.

By the numbers: Schwartz was approved 12-10, while Kaufman was approved 12-11.

Driving the news: Cassidy said he got a few concessions from HHS to justify his support for Kaufman, including promises of "key personnel changes and better oversight to ensure that science and not ideology is driving decision making."

  • "Mr. Kaufman has said some pretty stupid things and irresponsible things regarding immunization. He has owned up to that in his conversations with me," Cassidy said.
  • "I am assured that if he is confirmed, he will not be involved in vaccine policy."
  • Cassidy warned that "there will be future leverage points for this committee over future appointees if these commitments are not kept."

Between the lines: Neither nomination was a slam dunk. The votes were supposed to happen last week, but they had to be postponed because Republicans couldn't get enough senators to show up for the vote — and because they had more questions about Kaufman.

Context: Schwartz faced tough questioning during her July 15 confirmation hearing over whether she could steer clear of political interference and chart a course for the beleaguered public health agency.

  • While she vowed to "never betray the science" and rebuild trust in the CDC, Schwartz hedged on whether she would tell Congress if she was told to adopt "unscientific" or harmful policies, saying she didn't believe either President Trump or Kennedy would do that.
  • Schwartz was Trump's third nominee to lead the CDC, following Susan Monarez, who was fired after less than a month in the role claiming she was dismissed for refusing to rubber-stamp Kennedy's vaccine policies.
  • The former deputy surgeon general was viewed as a less polarizing pick than some of Trump's past health nominees. Public health experts have said she'd face challenges stabilizing an agency that's lacked a full-time political leader for almost a year and is beset by morale and staffing problems.

item.title: Election fears run rampant as November nears: poll
item.description:
Data: Charles F. Kettering Foundation and Gallup. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

Americans fear November's midterms could be stolen or otherwise compromised, with most worried about political pressure to change results or officials mishandling ballots, new Gallup polling finds.

Why it matters: President Trump has cast the American election system as under siege and vulnerable with unfounded claims about his 2020 loss. Meanwhile, his critics warn his push to reshape the ways Americans vote are undermining elections.

By the numbers: Republicans (56%) and Democrats (77%) alike fear politicians will pressure election officials to change the outcomes of races.

  • 80% report a great deal or fair amount of concern that political leaders will take actions they know are possibly illegal.
  • Nearly eight in 10 also worry about wealthy people or organizations making large, anonymous political donations (78%) or about gerrymandering (77%), as redistricting has reshaped the upcoming midterm elections.

Zoom in: Some fears are personal: 40% say they're concerned about being confronted, followed or recorded while voting.

  • And the anxiety is rampant: Nearly three-quarters (73%) report at least a fair amount of concern about multiple aspects of the election process, rather than just one fear.

The bottom line: In an election year that's sure to divide the already politically fractured country, Americans can at least agree on one thing: They're worried about their vote being safe.

Go deeper: Trump hits a wall on voter fraud
